yqjl0k.text: Headlines warn that AI could threaten humanity, and it’s easy to wave that off as science fiction. But the real danger is more ordinary and already here. Research published by Gen Threat Labs demonstrated how quickly an AI agent’s autonomy can become a liability. In a controlled experiment, researchers manipulated an agent through content it encountered while reading email, prompting it to execute system commands, transmit data outside its environment and perform destructive file operations. No software vulnerability was required. The agent simply treated untrusted content as instruction. That autonomy is expanding daily. Agents are moving from answering questions to taking action doing everything from executing code, connecting to services, managing files and making decisions on a user’s behalf. The shift from developer-focused tools like OpenClaw to widespread use of personal assistants like Muse, happened quickly. Delegating work across platforms is becoming commonplace and how people interact with AI. The risks extend beyond manipulating agents. In October, Gen Threat Labs documented Warden Stealer, malware targeting configuration files and local data associated with AI assistants and coding tools, potentially exposing credentials, access tokens and conversation histories. When software can act with a user’s permissions, trust can’t be reduced to whether a model produces a safe-sounding answer. People need to know what an agent can access, where it is connecting, what it is doing and whether the protection around it works. That is why Gen is building the Agent Trust Hub: a trust layer designed to extend protection across the agent lifecycle, from verification and visibility to runtime safety and enforcement. Trust starts before an agent acts Agentic systems gain capabilities through skills, plugins, tools and other integrations. These extensions make agents more useful, but they also expand risk by introducing hidden instructions, excessive permissions, and malicious code. Earlier this year, Gen researchers identified that 12% of skills available on ClawHub – at the time – were malicious. Many impersonated legitimate extensions while introducing instructions designed to trick agents into downloading malware. The Agent Trust Hub (ATH) helps assess these risks before a capability is installed or used. It brings together skill scanning, a curated marketplace of trusted skills and mechanisms that allow agents to check themselves for safety. Gen’s partnership with Vercel also brings verification and visible risk ratings into the skills.sh ecosystem, where developers discover and install new capabilities. Securing how agents connect Agents communicate across services, regions and websites, often at a speed and scale that traditional human-oriented controls were not designed to manage. VPN for Agents, a part of the ATH, addresses that connectivity gap with an AI-native VPN built for autonomous agents. Powered by Norton VPN infrastructure, it provides encrypted, private connectivity without requiring a conventional client installation. Its multi-tunnel design allows multiple agents to operate simultaneously through separate protected connections, including across different countries. The architecture gives people greater control over how agents communicate and helps protect an agent’s identity and location while it works. Putting guardrails between decision and execution Secure connectivity is necessary, but insufficient on its own. An agent may encounter a malicious web page, poisoned skill, prompt injection or hallucinated package after it has already been trusted and connected. Gen’s Sage is designed as a cross-agent safety layer for AI coding assistants. Using deterministic hook APIs, it can intercept shell commands, file operations and web requests before they run, rather than relying solely on instructions asking the model to be careful. Sage evaluates actions through multiple detection layers, including URL reputation, threat heuristics, prompt-injection detection and supply-chain checks. Depending on the result, it can allow an action, ask the user to decide or deny it. For example, if an agent setting up a project decides to download a script and immediately execute it, Sage can inspect that command before it runs. The approach provides a safety net across supported agents, including Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, OpenClaw and OpenCode. Inspecting actions before they execute Sage is also open source, allowing developers to inspect its operation, extend detection rules and build common interfaces across agent platforms. No single layer can catch every risk, and Sage doesn’t replace endpoint protection. Its focus is on the moment an agent’s autonomy becomes execution. That runtime approach also extends to consumers through Norton AI Agent Protection in Norton 360, which monitors supported agent activity and adds security controls between an agent’s decision and its execution. Coverage depends on the integration, because a security engine needs visibility into an action and a way to stop it. That practical limitation also led Gen to publish AARTS, the AI Agent Runtime Safety Standard, an open specification for how agent platforms can expose security events and enforce decisions from security engines. Making data practices easier to understand An assistant organizing a calendar needs calendar information. An agent managing an inbox needs access to messages. We’ve framed the question around agents: “Should they know anything about us,” when we should be asking whether users can understand and control what they share. The AI Data Checker adds that visibility layer to the Agent Trust Hub. People can submit an email address or username to help identify where that information may appear across AI services and connected accounts. They can then explore how services describe data collection, retention, personalization, advertising and model training. The tool can also analyze an AI app’s URL or terms page, translating dense policy language into more accessible information. Trust needs an independent yardstick The final part of a trust layer is measurement. Security providers shouldn’t ask people to rely on claims that can’t be independently checked. Gen initiated a collaboration with the Anti-Malware Testing Standards Organization (AMTSO) to develop guidelines for testing products that protect agentic systems. Published in September 2026, the guidelines establish a framework for repeatable, comparable evaluation across consumer and enterprise environments. Agentic attacks are not always files that can be dropped into a scanner. They can involve multi-turn prompt injection, tool misuse, malicious skills, plugins or MCP servers. Agents can also cause harm without an attacker, such as deleting the wrong files or exposing data after misunderstanding a task. The methodology therefore separates questions often blurred together: Did protection detect the threat? Did it prevent the action? Did the underlying model refuse on its own? Did protection block legitimate activity? It also calls for reproducible test cases, documented model versions, false-positive testing and empirical validation of vendor claims. Building confidence without slowing progress The agentic era does not need a single magic shield. It needs layered protection that can verify capabilities, secure connections, enforce guardrails, clarify data practices and demonstrate effectiveness through independent testing. When someone asks an agent to read their inbox, an email sender should have no authority over what it does next. Protecting that boundary is the job of a trust layer: keeping an agent working for the person who gave it access, even when someone else is trying to give it orders. Before you install your next skill or plugin, visit the Gen Agent Trust Hub and make sure your agent only takes orders from you. Sponsored and written by Gen Digital.

n4mo4b.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 23, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Attack Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a large-scale campaign that has targeted exposed network edge devices such as Fortinet FortiGate and Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect firewalls. "Artifacts from this investigation also indicate that operators in this campaign have obtained access to numerous organizations worldwide, and have attempted to further compromise some victims, resulting in persistent remote access and data exfiltration," according to a joint investigation published by Group-IB and NyxLab. The widespread exploitation activity has been attributed to a threat actor known as k0t, who also goes by the aliases CryptoFeel, Member19, and QazWsxShop. The cybercriminal actor was first seen in the wild on October 22, 2025. The threat actor is assessed to share connections with ransomware groups such as Qilin and The Gentlemen, likely operating as an initial access broker or an affiliate. Analysis of the threat actor's dark web activity reveals a keen interest in purchasing vulnerability exploit code and tools or premium accounts for metadata search engines like FOFA and ZoomEye. The campaign's victims are global and belong to a broad range of sectors, given the indiscriminate targeting of exposed network devices. A significant chunk of compromises are said to have taken place between February and June 2026, which also overlaps with another credential harvesting campaign codenamed FortiBleed. Nearly 38% of victims are concentrated in the Asia Pacific region, followed by 31.9% in Latin America, 15.8% in Europe, and 12.7% in the Middle East and North Africa. The attack chain plays out as follows - Conduct reconnaissance through public scanning tools like FOFA and ZoomEye to enumerate internet-facing VPN and firewall appliances, filter candidates by product, and put together target lists of potentially vulnerable edge devices. Attempt to exploit these devices via known vulnerabilities like CVE-2025-64446 (a path traversal flaw in FortiWeb) and CVE-2026-0257 (an authentication bypass flaw in Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS and Prisma Access) through bespoke Python scripts named "fortnew.py" and "exploit_2026_0257.py," or perform brute-force attacks using common username and password combinations, to obtain initial access. Establish a foothold on the targets via an OpenConnect VPN connection. Conduct post-exploitation actions and additional credential theft like enumeration of Active Directory, SMB, and installed antivirus solution. Establish persistence on the host via legitimate remote access tools like MeshCentral Agent, Atera, Teramind, and AnyDes, as well as an open-source, adversary-emulation framework known as AdaptixC2. Exfiltrate harvested data using Rclone into Wasabi S3 buckets and MEGA cloud drives. The attacks are also characterized by the use of legitimate administrator and pentesting utilities like NetExec, SoftPerfect, Impacket, noPac, Kerbrute, PetitPotam, and Mimikatz to burrow deeper into victims' corporate environments. "k0t appears to select potential targets by enumerating exposed network appliances at scale rather than researching individual organizations," Group-IB and NyxLab researchers said. "His stated geographic priorities begin with the United States and Canada, followed by European countries and selected APAC markets." "The product and location of an exposed device therefore appear to matter more than the industry of the organization operating it, consistent with the broad range of victims observed in this campaign." k0t's links to Qilin and The Gentlemen stem from the fact that many victims of the campaign were also later listed by the ransomware groups on their data leak sites. However, the exact nature of the connection between the threat and these gangs is unclear. What's more, Group-IB and NyxLab said they found a "negligible overlap" in compromised data between this activity and FortBleed. More than 70,000 exposed credentials associated with network devices and LDAP dumps have been identified in connection with the campaign. "This aligns with reports that many operators are likely to be involved in the FortiBleed activity cluster, suggesting that this may be a separate dataset, operator subset, or related access operation within the broader FortiBleed-related activity," the researchers said. "Organisations are advised to act on ensuring that any vulnerabilities mentioned in this report are appropriately remedied."

jkr7vn.text: The British government proposed on Thursday introducing prison sentences of up to 14 years and unlimited fines for damaging undersea cables and pipelines. It comes amid growing concerns over the vulnerability of subsea cables to so-called “hybrid warfare” by hostile states, including physical and cyberattacks targeting the cables themselves or the installations and digital systems on land. According to the consultation’s white paper, the new criminal offenses would cover telecommunications cables, electricity interconnectors and pipelines carrying 99% of the U.K.’s international data traffic and supplying 74% of its gas. The proposals would replace the Submarine Telegraph Act 1885, a Victorian-era law that carries a maximum fine of £1,000 — a fraction of the repair costs — and five years’ imprisonment in cases of deliberate damage. Repairs to the Estlink 2 electricity cable between Finland and Estonia — damaged by the anchor of the Eagle S oil tanker on Christmas Day 2024 — were estimated by grid operator Elering at €50 million to €60 million ($56 million to $67 million). Attempts to prosecute senior officers of that ship are ongoing. Under the new proposed law, alongside the 14 years for those found guilty of deliberate damage, perpetrators of reckless damage would face up to 10 years in prison and those of gross negligence up to two years. The government said it plans to introduce statutory security and resilience requirements for subsea telecommunications operators, with powers to direct cable and repair providers on national security grounds. Separate rules would govern fiber-optic sensing technology, which can detect activity at sea but could expose sensitive information. Telecoms minister Ian Murray and energy minister Michael Shanks said in a joint foreword that the risks to critical subsea infrastructure was involving, citing a warning earlier this year that a Royal Navy attack submarine had surfaced near a Russian spy ship mapping this infrastructure in British waters. Matt Western, the chair of Parliament’s Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy, welcomed the proposals, stating “the legislation covering attacks on undersea cables was written in a different age and it is right that a White Paper has been brought forward to bring it up to date.” Questions over jurisdiction in incidents of cable damage have complicated prosecutions elsewhere, alongside questions over whether they were truly reckless accidents or intentional attempts by Russia to undermine Europe. Finnish investigators initially suspected deliberate damage, but officials from several North Sea and Baltic countries later told Recorded Future News they increasingly believed that incident and other Baltic Sea cable breaks were accidental, citing investigations, intelligence and shipping data. The British government says the country’s cable network remains highly resilient and that most faults result from anchors, fishing nets, environmental hazards or technical failures while also warning of growing suspicious activity. In April, the Ministry of Defence said British and allied forces had tracked a Russian attack submarine and vessels linked to Russia’s Main Directorate of Deep Sea Research, or GUGI, near cables and pipelines north of Britain, allegedly mapping such infrastructure for potential wartime sabotage. The 12-week public consultation closes January 14, 2027. No previous articleNo new articlesAlexander Martin is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

s512s3.text: A key system used by Quest Diagnostics to manage medical test results was taken offline on Thursday after the company discovered unauthorized access. The company published a statement and an FAQ about the cyberattack, warning customers that they “believe some patient data” within the system was accessed. The platform, Quanum Lab Services Manager (LSM), is used to place test orders as well as receive and look up results. Access to the system has been paused while Quest investigates the attack. No other part of Quest has been impacted by the cyberattack but several other systems were paused as investigators probe the breach. Quest said it is working with law enforcement to resolve the incident and is investigating what patient data was affected by the attack. Customers can use paper requisitions in place of the system and Quest pledged to have Quantum back up and running by Friday. The company noted in the release that the incident did not involve the recent PHP vulnerabilities causing alarm among cybersecurity experts. A Quest spokesperson declined to comment on the nature of the incident. Quest is one of the largest clinical laboratory companies in the U.S., reporting more than $11 billion in revenue last year. The New Jersey-based company says it serves half of the doctors and hospitals in the U.S. and one in three American adults each year. No hacking group has taken credit for the incident as of Thursday afternoon. Quest is one of several healthcare testing firms to report cyber incidents in 2026. Baylor Genetics recently admitted that a data breach impacted more than 2.8 million of its patients and exposed lab results, medical testing information, Social Security numbers and more. Several other electronic health records companies dealt with attacks this year. In response to the attacks and several others over the last two years, Congress passed a bill this month expanding federal cyber requirements for healthcare organizations that handle patient data.

1gfr9c.text: Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) released security updates to patch 72 vulnerabilities in the Aruba Operating System (ArubaOS), including eight maximum-severity authentication bypass and code execution issues. Also known as AOS, ArubaOS powers Aruba Networking enterprise wireless infrastructure, including mobility conductors, access points, controllers, and gateway devices. The eight maximum-severity security flaws patched today affect multiple AOS-8 and AOS-10 software versions, and they can be exploited by remote threat actors without privileges through low-complexity attacks that don't require user interaction. HPE warned customers to patch these security issues as soon as possible and provided mitigation measures, including restricting access to AOS management interfaces. "Customers are strongly urged to patch their instances due to the complexity, breadth, and impact of these vulnerabilities," the company warned in a Thursday security advisory. "To minimize the likelihood of an attacker exploiting these vulnerabilities, HPE Networking recommends that the CLI and web-based management interfaces be restricted to a dedicated layer 2 segment/VLAN and/or controlled by firewall policies at layer 3 and above along with accounting controls for tracking and logging user activities and resource usage." The full list of maximum severity flaws fixed today can be found in the table embedded below: CVE-ID Vulnerability CVE-2026-79844 Authentication Bypass Leading to RCE in AOS-10 CVE-2026-79845 Authentication Bypass in the PAPI Protocol of AOS-10 CVE-2026-79846 Unauthenticated Command Injection in AOS-8 CVE-2026-79847 Unauthenticated Buffer Overflow leads to RCE in AOS-10 CVE-2026-79848 Unauthenticated SQL Injection leading to RCE in AOS-8 CVE-2026-79849 Unauthenticated SQL Injection leading to RCE in AOS-8 CVE-2026-79850 Authentication Bypass leading to RCE in AOS-8 CVE-2026-79851 Unauthenticated Buffer Overflow leading to RCE in AOS-10 The company added that it has not yet found publicly available proof-of-concept exploit code or evidence that these vulnerabilities are being exploited in the wild. "HPE Networking is not aware of any public discussion or exploit code that targets the listed vulnerabilities as of the release date of this advisory," it said. In June 2025, HPE patched eight critical StoreOnce vulnerabilities that allowed authentication bypass and remote code execution and, one month later, warned of hardcoded credentials in Aruba Instant On Access Points that can let attackers bypass device authentication. In January 2025, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) also flagged a maximum-severity HPE OneView vulnerability as exploited in attacks. More recently, HPE warned of critical flaws allowing admin password resets and remote code execution on unpatched AOS-CX devices. HPE employs more than 61,000 people worldwide and provides services and products to over 55,000 enterprise customers worldwide, including 90% of Fortune 500 companies. Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.The Blue Report 2026 measures defenses technique by technique across 338 million simulations run in customer production environments. Get the report

10pw4j3.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 23, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security PHP has warned of another way an attacker could run code on a web server, two days after it shipped emergency fixes for the critical PHP2Shell flaws. The new issue, assigned CVE-2026-115560, affects only web applications configured in an unusual way, and PHP considers it an unlikely risk. The project is not issuing an emergency fix for it. Instead, it recommends turning off a feature called session upload progress until a fix is available in the next routine release. The warning came in a short informational advisory published on October 23. It follows the October 21 emergency release that fixed two critical PHP2Shell flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which let an attacker without an account run code on a server. Those were patched in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. The new issue is separate and is not fixed by those releases. Only a narrow setup is at risk. PHP says the problem can occur when a web application does all of the following: sets the session.serialize_handler option to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration, then changes that option to php while running by calling ini_set(), and makes that change before it calls session_start(). Session upload progress must also still be turned on. An application that never changes the serialize handler while running can leave the feature on and is not exposed through this path. PHP says this setup is unlikely in practice. The action is one line. PHP recommends setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next routine bugfix release. This is the same setting it already listed as a mitigation in the October 21 advisory for CVE-2026-109619. Anyone who applied it then and left it in place needs to do nothing more for the new issue. Session upload progress is turned on by default and lets an application track the progress of a file upload. Because the setup is uncommon, PHP is handling the fix as part of its regular release cycle rather than as an emergency, and it will publish a full advisory for CVE-2026-115560 with the next release. PHP has not stated which versions are affected, which releases will contain the fix, or a severity score. It also has not said whether the new issue shares a root cause with CVE-2026-109619. No exploitation of CVE-2026-115560 has been reported; the attacks reported since October 21 target the two earlier PHP2Shell flaws. Separately, attempts to exploit the two earlier PHP2Shell flaws have surged. Amazon said its honeypots logged an exploit attempt against CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 on October 17, four days before the flaws were disclosed, and Cloudflare said attempts rose from tens of thousands within 45 minutes of the October 21 disclosure to millions by early October 22.Attackers have tried to use the flaws to install a Mirai botnet variant, according to Sophos and Arctic Wolf. Those attempts have so far failed: Previdian, Wordfence and others report scanning and probing but no confirmed code execution, and researchers say a reliable exploit is proving harder to build than expected. That activity targets the two flaws patched on October 21, not CVE-2026-115560, which has not been reported under attack.

1tjtc5m.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 23, 2026Malware / Cyber Espionage The Russian state-sponsored hacking group Sandworm teamed up with another threat actor to carry out a destructive wiping attack targeting a Ukrainian logistics company last year. According to ESET, the attack involved UAC-0099 (aka Earth Sirrush) obtaining initial access to the target on July 16, 2025, via a spear-phishing email bearing a malware-laced attachment that led to the deployment of the MATCHWOK backdoor via a downloader called MATCHBOIL. The activity ultimately culminated with the threat actor handing off access to Sandworm, which then conducted a data-wiping attack on September 17, 2025, more than two months after it obtained a foothold. What makes the attack stand out is UAC-0099's use of a previously undocumented backdoor called MythicRatatoskr that communicates with a command-and-control (C2) server hosted inside the Yggdrasil mesh network. The backdoor was deployed a day after MATCHWOK was executed. There are indications that development on the backdoor started sometime between December 2024 and February 2025. Its functionality is fairly straightforward in that it sends victim metadata to the C2 server, poll for new commands, transmit command output, take screenshots, and upload/download files. It can also alter the current working directory, enumerate directory contents, change the C2 server URL, execute a shell command via "cmd.exe," and spawn a reverse SOCKS5 proxy. In addition, some artifacts include a 10-minute startup delay in a likely effort to avoid immediately connecting to the Yggdrasil network and evade detection. "To our knowledge, this is the first documented case of Yggdrasil being abused in this way by a state-aligned threat actor, and it may signal a broader trend of adversaries adopting experimental peer-to-peer networks to increase the resilience and stealth of their infrastructure," ESET researchers Anton Cherepanov and Peter Strýček said. MythicRatatoskr is said to have been used to deploy a SOCKS5 server to route connections through the compromised network. The attack culminated with Sandworm carrying out a data-wiping attack by dropping the SDelete utility via Active Directory Group Policy. It's worth noting that the Sandworm-linked NikoWiper malware is also derived from SDelete. Yggdrasil map with the C&C serve While the attack investigated by ESET compromised a Windows system, source code references to "crond" within MythicRatatoskr suggest there possibly exists an equivalent Linux version of the malware. The assessment that UAC-0099 is likely collaborating with Sandworm is not new. In its APT Activity Report Q2 2025–Q3 2025, ESET said it observed UAC-0099 conducting initial access operations and subsequently transferring "validated targets" to Sandworm for further post-exploitation. These attacks targeted government, energy, logistics, and grain sectors in Ukraine, the Slovak cybersecurity company noted at the time. This sort of cooperation between Russia-aligned actors is also not new. Last year, ESET said it identified evidence that Gamaredon and Turla were working together to target and co-compromise Ukrainian entities, with one intrusion leveraging Gamaredon's PteroGraphin to deploy Turla's Kazuar backdoor. Furthermore, a Gamaredon-linked downloader called Pterodo has been used to retrieve and execute InvisiMole, a modular spyware program put to use against targets in Ukraine and Russia. "This kind of cooperation underscores the potential for coordinated cyber espionage campaigns among Russia-aligned groups, likely intended to amplify their operational impact," ESET said.

1se2rnk.text: Pillow, the most widely used image library for Python, can be made to run operating system commands on a server by specifying the name of a file it is told to open. The flaw, CVE-2026-112900, is in the way Pillow handles EPS images, which it opens by passing the file's name to Ghostscript, a separate program it runs to turn the image into pixels, without checking the name first. Ghostscript can read a name chosen by an attacker as instructions rather than as a file, and point it to a second file that carries commands to run. Pillow's maintainers fixed it in version 13.0.0, released on October 16. Pillow turns up almost everywhere Python handles images: web upload forms, avatar and thumbnail tools, document and PDF pipelines, and most machine-learning projects pull it in. OX Security, the firm whose report drew attention to the flaws, estimates the library is downloaded about 436 million times a month. Version 13.0.0 is a large security release, with fixes across four severity levels, from low to critical, two of which are rated critical by the maintainers. None of the flaws is known to be under attack. The weakness is the filename, not the picture. "The flaw is triggered by the filename, not by anything in the PostScript document," the advisory says, meaning a harmless EPS file can still cause damage when an attacker sets its name. That makes upload endpoints that keep or build a stored file's name from user input the realistic target. The flaw only reaches Ghostscript on hosts that have the gs program installed, which Pillow needs to open EPS at all. It affects Pillow from version 2.6.0 up to 12.3.0. The maintainers rate it moderate, because the attacker has to control the filename. The CVE record assigned by GitHub rates it 9.2 out of 10 and marks it as the same condition. Two of the fixes sit in the maintainers' top "critical" tier. One is a separate memory bug, described in the release notes as stale image data reused after a mode change. The other covers two overflow flaws in Pillow's JPEG decoding. One of those JPEG flaws, in the FlashPix (FPX) format, was shown to run an attacker's command from a single call to Image.open() on a crafted file, as long as the optional olefile package is installed. Pillow recognizes these files by their content, not their extension, so a server that opens untrusted uploads can be hit with no user action. The other, CVE-2026-112403, overflows a memory buffer when a program makes a thumbnail of a crafted lossless JPEG. Its advisory reports a crash, not code execution. The bug was "found by Anthropic using Claude to study the security of open-source software, validated manually by Ada Logics," the advisory says, part of a wider effort by the company that has turned up hundreds of flaws in open-source libraries. A third flaw, CVE-2026-112393, has been in Pillow since 2013. It overflows a memory buffer when a program saves a compressed TIFF image to memory rather than to a file on disk, the common pattern for a service that re-encodes an upload and hands it back. The advisory says the reporters crashed the process with it, and turned it into code execution only with the help of a second, separate flaw that leaked memory addresses. Saving to a real file on disk is not affected. The CVE records, assigned by GitHub, score the EPS, TIFF, and JPEG-thumbnail flaws 9.2 out of 10, a critical rating. Each depends on conditions the score does not carry, and the maintainers' own ratings for the batch run from moderate to critical. In the CVE records, CISA's analysts mark no known exploitation for the EPS flaw and a public proof of concept for the TIFF one. What to do Upgrade to Pillow 13.0.0, which fixes all of these, and rebuild any containers, wheels, or base images that bundle an older copy. Pillow 13 drops Python 3.10, so installs still on 3.10 need Python 3.11 or newer as well. pip install -U "Pillow>=13.0.0" Until you can upgrade, Pillow's security guidance and the advisories point to steps that cut each path: EPS / Ghostscript: keep the gs program off any host that processes untrusted uploads, and never pass an attacker-controlled filename to Image.open() for EPS. JPEG thumbnails: avoid draft() and thumbnail() on untrusted JPEGs, or call load() first, or pass reducing_gap=None. TIFF: treat saving a TIFF to an in-memory buffer such as io.BytesIO as a sensitive path when the image came from a user.

1ukioqa.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 23, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security Malicious Brotli data can make an application on an official build of Node.js run attacker-supplied code, security researchers at Imperva have demonstrated. Their "Node2Shell" proof of concept ran code on the official Node.js 24.22.0 image for Linux arm64, with no debugger or custom build, by feeding crafted data to the bundled Brotli decoder (CVE-2026-111497). Node.js disclosed the flaw and released fixes on October 21, and applications that decode untrusted Brotli data should update. Imperva's test did not succeed on every attempt, and code execution took several tries in its Linux arm64 setup. The result covers that one build and application setup, with other architectures and the 22.x and 26.x lines not tested. On the fixed release, 24.22.1, the same data was rejected, and no code ran. The demonstration goes beyond the first public proof of concept, which achieved code execution only on a deliberately weakened test build. On a standard build, that proof of concept's author reported a crash and a limited read of process memory, not code execution, and said a working attack on a normal build was not achieved. No exploitation of the flaw in the wild has been reported as of October 22. Which Applications Are Affected The flaw is in the Brotli decoder that Node.js bundles, so it affects applications on the 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x lines, not only the one build Imperva tested. A service reaches that decoder from either side of an HTTP exchange: when it reads a Brotli-compressed response through Node.js's built-in fetch(), or when middleware decodes a Brotli-compressed request body. Express 5's body parsers, such as express.json(), express.urlencoded(), express.text() and express.raw(), now decode Brotli request bodies when applied to a route, alongside gzip and deflate. A plain Node.js HTTP server does not decode a Brotli request body just by receiving one, so the decoding needs that middleware or an explicit call. Imperva reproduced code execution through both the request-body and response paths, testing Express 5.0.0 to 5.3.0 and body-parser 2.0.0 to 2.3.0 at pinned versions, and did not test every release in between. How the Bug Works Imperva traced the cause to how the decoder handles an impossible point in a Brotli stream: the stream announces the block types it will use as decoding runs, and the test input reached a block change that the stream's own structure ruled out. The vulnerable decoder read that as a request for more input and kept going in an invalid state. In a separate test with a memory sanitizer, continuing from that state wrote past an intended buffer, the out-of-bounds write behind the flaw. Node.js fixed the flaw by importing an upstream Brotli patch that makes the decoder stop with a format error at that point instead of continuing. What to Do The fix is to move to a patched release. The update should reach container images and other artifacts that bundle a Node binary, which a package inventory can miss. End-of-life lines 20.x and earlier do not receive the fix and should be moved to a supported line. The advisory lists no workaround inside Node.js, so an application that cannot update at once has no fallback in the runtime. Imperva suggested limiting untrusted Brotli traffic on affected paths where that is practical, and said only the update removes the flaw. The company also added rules to its own web application firewall and tested them against the attacks it reproduced. Vercel, which runs Node.js for its customers, said it added rules on October 21 that block the attack in inbound requests. The rules do not cover Brotli responses an application fetches from other servers, and do not replace updating.

1nw9arq.text: AI agents paying for API calls with the x402 SDKs could sign a payment for their full balance of a supported token if a malicious API asked for it, security firm V12 said on October 22. The cause was the SDKs' default client, which set no spending limit until releases on August 18 added one. The risk was limited to agents who automatically signed payments and whose apps set no limits. The missing limit is one of 25 flaws V12 found in the x402 code, and one of three it rated critical and described in detail. The x402 Foundation, which maintains the SDKs, had already fixed all three critical flaws in the August 18 releases. One of the other two let a facilitator, the service that checks x402 payments, accept a Solana transaction that moved no tokens as a valid payment. Among the x402 SDKs, only the TypeScript one had this flaw. The other let a malicious server get an agent to sign a login message for a different website. V12 found the flaws by reviewing the code and running local tests. Neither V12 nor the x402 Foundation has publicly reported any attacks using them. The foundation has published no security advisory for the three flaws, and its changelogs list the fixes without calling them security fixes. As of October 23, npm audit returned no advisories for the last TypeScript releases before the fixes, and PyPI listed no vulnerabilities for the last Python release before them, The Hacker News found. A developer who relies on those checks gets no warning to upgrade. Coinbase created x402 and handed it to the x402 Foundation this year, a Linux Foundation project whose members include Visa and Mastercard. Coinbase holds the most senior seat on the foundation's technical steering committee. No Spending Limit in the Default Client x402 is an open standard that lets software, including AI agents, pay for an API call within the web request itself, without requiring a person to approve each payment. A server that wants payment answers with the HTTP status code 402 Payment Required and lists its payment options, each with an amount, a token, and a recipient. The client picks one, signs a payment, and sends the request again. The default client took the first option on the list, and before the fix, it set no limit on the amount. A hostile API could use that to turn a routine data request into a request for the wallet's full balance of a supported token, V12 said. An earlier small payment could reveal the wallet address, so the server could look up the balance first. With an automatic signer and no payment policy set by the app, the client could sign a payment for that amount. For a token that supports signed transfers, the attacker could then submit the signed payment and collect the funds. The August 18 releases added spend controls to the TypeScript, Python, and Go clients. By default, they now cap each payment at $1 and allow only US dollar stablecoins the SDK recognizes, such as USDC. Token Approvals Accepted as Solana Payments In x402, a merchant's server relies on a facilitator to check each payment and submit it to the blockchain. On Solana, the facilitator also pays the transaction fee. The TypeScript facilitator code for Solana checked that a payment called an allowed token program, then read it as a transfer without checking the instruction type. A token approval, which lets another account spend tokens later but moves none itself, differs from a transfer only in its first byte. In V12's local test, the facilitator accepted such an approval as a valid payment. The test did not send a live transaction. A merchant relying on the facilitator could therefore deliver a paid resource while receiving no tokens, V12 said, calling it "a complete payment bypass." The attacker needed a token account, but no balance, and the facilitator paid the transaction fee each time. The Python and Go SDKs already checked the instruction type. The August 18 releases added the same check to the TypeScript code. Every published @x402/svm release from 2.0.0 to 2.22.0 lacks the check, and every release from 2.23.0 on has it, The Hacker News found by searching the published packages. Logins Signed for Other Websites x402 also has a sign-in extension called Sign-In-With-X (SIWx). It lets an agent log in by signing a short message with its wallet, for example to prove an earlier payment instead of paying again. On Ethereum, the message names the website, the wallet address, and a one-time code. The automated client signed these messages without verifying that the website named in them was the one it had contacted. A malicious server could get a fresh login message from another site, pass it to the agent, and use the signature to log in to that site as the agent's wallet, V12 said. That would work wherever the other site accepted the relayed message, and the attacker would get whatever access the login allowed. The August 18 releases make the TypeScript, Python and Go clients refuse to sign unless the site in the message matches the site that sent the 402 response. The project also changed the SIWx specification, which now says a client must refuse to sign when the two do not match. TypeScript code that calls createSIWxPayload directly must now pass the URL of the 402 response, after any redirects. The @x402/fetch and @x402/axios wrappers pass it on their own. What to Update Upgrading to the latest releases also brings later fixes, including one for a separate payment bypass in @x402/core 2.27.0 in September. As of October 23, the latest versions are 2.28.0 for @x402/core, @x402/svm, @x402/extensions, @x402/fetch and @x402/axios, v2.28.0 for the Go module and 2.25.0 for the Python package. In TypeScript, clients get the spending fix by updating @x402/fetch or @x402/axios to 2.23.0 or later, which pulls in the matching @x402/core. Apps that use SIWx also need @x402/extensions 2.23.0 or later, which holds the login check. Facilitators that check Solana payments need @x402/svm 2.23.0 or later. After the upgrade, existing clients are capped at $1 per payment and limited to recognized stablecoins unless the app sets its own spend controls. Apps that pass spendControls: false turn all of these controls off. Teams that cannot upgrade yet can register a payment policy that drops any option above a set amount. The older clients support this with registerPolicy in TypeScript and Go and register_policy in Python, which also has a ready-made max_amount policy. V12 advises clients to check that a SIWx login message identifies the site they contacted before signing, to set budgets for each payment and in total, and to limit which tokens, networks, and recipients they will pay.

c3imod.text: Threat actors have been observed unsuccessfully attempting to exploit the newly disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to rope infected systems into a Mirai botnet variant called Potassium, as it emerges that weaponizing the flaws may be harder than previously thought. The attacks aim to exploit CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS scores: 9.2), which can result in unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) via specially crafted HTTP requests. The vulnerabilities have been patched in PHP versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. "However, analysis of the sample revealed that it is an updated and significantly expanded version of the Mirai-derived botnet variant identified in early 2026," Sophos said. "The sample displays downloader and network disruption functionality." Specifically, it resolves a hard-coded, encrypted command-and-control (C2) address, establishes a TCP connection to 134.199.154[.]64, and sends an HTTP request. The malware then checks for an HTTP 200 response status and verifies that the resulting payload begins with the ELF magic bytes 7F 45 4C 46, indicating that it expects a Linux ELF binary as a follow-on payload. "A resolver function supports IPv4 addresses and hostname resolution, with additional fallback resolution logic that includes hard-coded public DNS servers such as 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1, and 1.0.0.1," Sophos added. "As with Mirai malware historically, this sample can execute DDoS attacks." The attacks have been found to originate from the following three IP addresses - 85.11.167[.]243 217.60.242[.]76 45.198.224[.]169 These attack sources have been found to contact 92.118.112[.]100 to retrieve a loader, which is responsible for deploying the Mirai botnet variant. Further analysis of the artifact within a network-contained sandbox has revealed that the botnet issues a DNS query for thunder.godofthunder[.]st, resolves it to 134.199.154[.]64, and establishes a C2 channel on TCP port 50792. The end goal is to launch sustained volumetric flood attacks against two adjacent hosts located within a single Ukrainian network - 45.88.138[.]0 45.88.138[.]44 The lack of a successful attack leveraging PHP2Shell in the wild suggests that threat actors are "struggling" to come up with reliable exploits, Sophos added. Potassium was first flagged by botnet tracking platform Synthient in March 2026. In a follow-up analysis, Nokia Deepfield researchers described the malware as a Mirai fork which uses "ChaCha20 for the static config table (the first time we have seen ChaCha20 used this way in a Mirai variant), a single static byte (0xED) for everything on the wire, a named reverse-shell protocol (SHELL / SHOUT) on the same channel as attack commands, and a DNS misdirection scheme that swaps the two 16-bit halves of every resolved A record before connect()." Arctic Wolf, which also shared additional details of the same weaponized PHP2Shell exploitation attempt, said the botnet supports 24 commands to facilitate flood attacks over ICMP, TCP, UDP, and OpenVPN protocol. Both builds for ARM and x86 also contain configuration for resolving C2 infrastructure through Ethereum Name Service (ENS). "ENS resolution was disabled in both samples, indicating that the capability was present but inactive," the cybersecurity firm said. "If enabled in future variants, it could complicate disruption by reducing reliance on registrars and DNS providers, requiring defenders to block the ENS names, RPC infrastructure, and resolved command-and-control addresses." Threat Actor Mass Exploits PHP2Shell The development comes as SOCRadar said it found PHP2Shell exploit tooling for PHP 8.4.26 on an exposed attacker-controlled server ("206.188.197[.]105:9999"), alongside three screening scripts that check live websites for preconditions the PHP2Shell chain depends on. The scripts, according to the cybersecurity company, checked about 20 public websites for the PHP version, server setup, and session settings the exploit needs. These websites span Canada, China, Finland, France, Poland, the U.K., and the U.S. "The central file, aslr_exploit.py, is a Python exploit the operator labels a 'one-click' PHP2Shell exploit for PHP 8.4.26 under Apache mod_php," SOCRadar said. "It works entirely over ordinary HTTP requests in three broad steps: it recycles the target's PHP worker, leaks memory addresses through the session cookie to defeat address space layout randomization (ASLR), and then abuses PHP's session upload progress handling to run a shell command." ASLR, short for Address Space Layout Randomization, is a cybersecurity mechanism that randomizes the memory locations used by system files and programs each time they are run, making it harder for attackers to predict where code will load. This built-in defense helps defend against memory-based exploits, such as buffer-overflow attacks. The other three companion scripts are as follows - php2shell_fp.py, which reads PHP version and server setup from about 20 sites deep_probe.py, which examines 11 of those sites for visible errors, phpinfo pages, file inclusion, and session injection to ascertain whether they meet exploit prerequisites wp_attack.py, which focuses on five WordPress sites to conduct user and plugin enumeration That said, there is no evidence of shell access on any screened site as of October 22, 2026, indicating the targeted sites did not meet the exploit's preconditions. The toolset is assessed to be part of a broader operation that involves the attacker extracting API keys and backend URLs from websites' client-side JavaScript, systematically sweeping web and API routes for unauthenticated access, and using a pool of rotating proxies to spread traffic and evade rate limits and blocking. "Related artifacts on the server additionally point to web-archive reconnaissance and automated CAPTCHA solving," SOCRadar noted. "Taken together, the toolset points to a financially motivated actor focused on cryptocurrency and Web3 targets." The same exploitation server ("206.188.197[.]105") has also been flagged by Hunt.io, which said the threat actor behind the operation has targeted 123 servers across cloud, shared-hosting and ISP networks. "About 57 run PHP, many on unsupported 5.x to 7.x," the threat intelligence firm said. "Ten rejected the request outright, including three of the five sitting behind Cloudflare. None was exploited." In all, 10 open directories hold PHP2Shell-related tooling - 206.188.197[.]105 102.210.149[.]166 122.10.110[.]72, 122.10.17[.]49 58.221.60[.]160:8000 41.223.30[.]7, 157.230.117[.]70 104.219.251[.]31 107.150.31[.]151 217.160.132[.]82 47.100.125[.]108, 54.169.109[.]7, 139.162.165[.]136 Defeating ASLR Protections The disclosure also coincides with the development of a PHP2Shell exploit that can achieve remote code execution on ASLR-enabled x86-64 systems with PHP's recommended production configuration. "One of the biggest obstacles has been address space layout randomization (ASLR), a protection designed to make memory corruption vulnerabilities much harder to exploit," Spencer McIntyre, director of exploit development at VulnCheck, told The Hacker News. "Our team developed a novel technique [...] that chains the two vulnerabilities together, using a memory leak to bypass ASLR and achieve remote code execution on x86-64 systems, even with PHP's recommended production error-display setting."ir "We haven't identified another public or commercial exploit that achieves this under the same conditions. Developing this capability was far from trivial, but it demonstrates that a major barrier to exploiting PHP2Shell on production-configured systems can be overcome." Consequences of successful exploitation of the flaws are severe, as it permits an attacker to execute code with the permissions of the web application, potentially gaining access to API keys, database connections, and other internal services the application can reach, VulnCheck said. "An attacker doesn't necessarily need administrator or root access to cause significant damage," McIntyre said. "Access to a vulnerable web application could provide a foothold into other parts of an organization's infrastructure." Exploit Attempts Plenty, None Successful The findings dovetail with reports indicating that broad exploitation attempts targeting the flaws are underway, including by a China-based IP address that has been observed trying to drop a web shell via a server-side session file. Web infrastructure company Cloudflare said it observed tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the flaw 45 minutes after the flaws were publicly announced, before climbing to hundreds of thousands within 2 hours and millions as of early October 22, 2026. "So far, most of the activity is scanning, along with some uncoordinated attempts to deliver various payloads," Cisco Talos said. "This is expected: scanning or basic exploitation with public proof-of-concept (PoC) code takes far less effort than integrating a vulnerability into an actor's own tooling." Data from Previdian's telemetry has so far recorded hundreds of exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-109618 from dozens of IP addresses, and against CVE-2026-109619 to a lesser degree. The first exploit event aimed at CVE-2026-109618 was recorded on October 21, 2026, at 1:05 p.m. UTC. "We've seen plenty of PHP2Shell probes and exploitation attempts in our honeypots," Previdian said. "At the time of writing, we've observed no successful remote code execution and no dropped PHP files. Reliable RCE may be harder to achieve than initially expected." This assessment has also been echoed by Beelzebub, Dataminr, and Wordfence, with observed activity so far limited to scanning, fingerprinting, and attempts to confirm command execution, steal credentials and secrets from environment variables, install persistent access, and retrieve and execute a second-stage payload. Wordfence has shared the following IP addresses as among those attempting to exploit the flaws - 87.121.84[.]174 181.215.186[.]252 185.196.220[.]132 185.161.210[.]29 152.233.51[.]69 45.134.225[.]16 107.189.14[.]87 193.47.62[.]24 2409:40d2:204e:4be:2a1f:f9c9:a055:e00b 103.147.220[.]17 The severity of the flaws has also led to several government, school and hospital websites going offline across Asia, Europe, and North America out of an abundance of caution. The U.K. government has confirmed that 32 digital services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable, largely stemming from the precautionary shutdowns while security updates and mitigations were applied. The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has issued approximately 50,000 warnings to businesses and other organizations. "The vulnerable code dates back to PHP 5.4, released in 2012," the Sysdig Threat Research Team said. "The bugs live in the PHP engine, not within any application. For that reason, any WordPress, Drupal, or Joomla site with clean application code is still exposed." With the fixes not available for older versions of PHP, PHP2Shell is expected to have a long tail, along the lines of Log4Shell. According to estimates from Google-owned VirusTotal, about 272,000 hosts run a supported PHP branch (8.2 to 8.5), Organizations on PHP 7.4, 8.0, or 8.1 are advised to move to a supported branch, or use a distribution backport. Attack surface management platform Censys said it currently detects over 3.08 million hosts and 56.6 million web properties running PHP. Of these, more than 34.4 million PHP services are still assessed to be vulnerable as of October 23, 2026. "Many applications with web servers and similar will likely remain vulnerable until their respective vendors patch these items," Dataminr said. "The implications of this are that many organizations will likely remain vulnerable to some degree for far longer than when patches are directly applied to owned and managed applications."

18tfvgi.text: The two PHP vulnerabilities dominating headlines this week have left experts with a mixed bag of data to track. Multiple large companies have reported an explosion in attempted exploitation. But dozens of experts told Recorded Future News that none of the attempts have been successful and argued that most of the available proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits only work in ideal lab conditions — making mass exploitation unlikely as of Friday. Experts at Amazon drew headlines on Thursday with a report that they saw evidence of exploitation attempts dating back to October 17, days before news broke of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 — now known colloquially as PHP2Shell. Sophos reported and then retracted a report of successful exploitation, writing on Thursday evening that it was only seeing a “small number of failed exploitation attempts.” Google’s John Hultquist said his team has not validated exploitation in the wild and have no evidence of successful wide-scale exploitation, but he noted that “exploitation may have already begun in a limited fashion and the threat is viable and very serious.” Arctic Wolf said exploitation attempts it observed were linked to the Potassium botnet, while researchers at Cobalt saw attempts tied to a Mirai botnet. Other experts similarly reported exploitation attempts that sought to infect devices with malware and turn them into bots as part of a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) network. Spencer McIntyre, director of exploit development at VulnCheck, said the company also has seen firsthand exploit attempts but noted that many involve PoCs that are “garbage and nonfunctional.” The current PoCs floating around social media only work in developer and researcher environments or on production apps that do not represent how PHP is typically configured in real life, he said. Several incident responders said those attempting to exploit the bugs are being hung up by address space layout randomization (ASLR), a protection McIntyre said was designed to make memory corruption bugs harder to exploit. “There's a significant difference between demonstrating a vulnerability and developing an exploit that can overcome the security protections found in real-world environments,” he said. McIntyre noted that his team has developed a novel technique to bypass ASLR but they have not identified another public or commercial exploit that does the same. “Developing this capability was far from trivial, but it demonstrates that a major barrier to exploiting PHP2Shell on production-configured systems can be overcome,” McIntyre added. McIntyre and other experts warned that ASLR is not a permanent barrier to exploitation of the bugs and urged organizations to patch any vulnerable systems. What ‘exploitation’ means Marcus Hutchins, a noted cybersecurity expert at Expel, said the difficulty of developing a reliable exploit may buy defenders a bit of time but it is impossible to predict how long it will take threat actors to come up with something viable. In several social media posts and in comments to Recorded Future News, he argued there are two separate theories as to what companies mean when they are reporting “exploitation.” Some are reporting sophisticated, likely state-sponsored, threat actors doing targeted exploitation while others are simply cataloging attempted mass exploitation using lab-focused PoCs that do not work. “The second case matches the evidence I've personally seen,” Hutchins said. While ASLR is not a “significant barrier” to successful exploitation, it does hinder attempts at mass exploitation, he added. “Currently there are no reports that I've seen of [successful] mass exploitation, nor have I seen any mass exploitation myself. However, someone has built a scanner which can remotely identify vulnerable systems, so there are a bunch of internet-wide scan attempts ongoing,” Hutchins explained. “This means that should a fully-weaponized exploit become available, it's likely that several threat actors already have target lists containing publicly reachable unpatched systems ready to go.” Censys created a PHP2Shell dashboard that says as of October 22, there are more than 41 million Internet-facing PHP services on affected versions and about 1 million operating with a fixed release. Cobalt CISO Andrew Obadiaru said the lack of confirmed compromises shows how hard PHP2Shell is to weaponize but argued that the difficulty won’t last, highlighting VulnCheck’s reported exploit. “Attackers are refining their tooling in the open, so defenders should treat this quiet period as borrowed time,” he said, warning that attackers are fingerprinting servers to find the exact configurations their exploit needs. “Once a working technique moves from specialist tooling into botnet playbooks, defenders will have days, not weeks, to catch up.” No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

10in7c6.text: Cloud hosting provider Railway published an urgent warning to users after detecting suspicious activity on its systems that store customer environment variables earlier this week. The company says its investigation indicates that, in some cases, an unauthorized third party may have obtained decrypted variables and urges all users to proactively rotate secrets and credentials. “Our investigation to date indicates that an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted environment variables and, for some of them, obtained the decrypted contents,” Railway says. “Environment variables may contain secrets such as API keys or database and registry credentials,” the company clarifies. Railway is a cloud platform for developers to deploy and run applications, APIs, databases, and various backend services. It has around 4.8 million users and hosts more than 16 million services. The service stores deployment-related configuration settings and credentials in environment variables, which the incident exposed. Railway says the incident was part of a series of attacks targeting AI inference providers, which were notified directly and advised to revoke all their keys as a precaution. AI inference providers are services that run AI models and return answers to Railway-hosted applications. Although initial analysis suggests only a subset of users may be affected, Railway urges all users to immediately rotate environment variables and secrets stored on the platform, including private registry credentials, and check associated service logs for unusual activity. Railway also said it has paused all deployments until the investigation completes, so users cannot roll out new versions during this time. According to the latest status page update, as of October 22 at 08:44 UTC, Railway had restored builds for Pro and Enterprise workspaces, but deployments remained delayed, with many queued. Builds had not yet resumed for Hobby, Free, and Trial workspaces, with restoration planned in that order. Railway said it will directly notify users whose accounts are confirmed to be compromised and provide further details. 1mjpt8y.text: A Toronto crime prevention program that long promised witnesses a safe space to anonymously report tips froze its operations late Wednesday night, hours after a Canadian news outlet reported that more than 1.5 million tips from Crime Stoppers chapters across the country were exposed in a data breach. Crime Stoppers urges people not to provide their names when submitting information, but reporters at Canada’s CBC broadcaster were able to reach more than a dozen tipsters by reviewing the hacked data made available to them in March by Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets). About half of the 1.5 million leaked tips CBC studied — some dating back 25 years — contained personal information, the outlet reported. While Canadian Crime Stoppers Association and individual chapters, including Toronto’s, had confirmed the breach in the days after the hack, they offered no detail about what was exposed, blaming the lack of information on vendor Navigate360 and its subsidiary, P3 Global Intel. But late Wednesday night the Toronto chapter broke ranks with the national association, revealing a timeline showing what it knew and when along with an announcement that it will pause operations. “Since 1984, people in Toronto have come to Toronto Crime Stoppers because we promised they could stay anonymous,” Sean Sportun, chair of Toronto Crime Stoppers, said in a statement. “This week’s reporting shows that for some of them, that promise was broken. We are deeply sorry.” The Toronto organization said it has directed Navigate360 to immediately stop taking tips and no longer process any new information. It also has told Canada’s National Anonymous Call Centre to stop receiving and processing tips meant for Toronto Crime Stoppers, according to the statement. “Until we have a safer way to protect you, please do not send us tips by phone, online, or through the app,” the statement said. The organization is looking for a way to take tips on a truly anonymous basis, it said. “For more than 40 years, people in Toronto have relied on Crime Stoppers to share what they know without giving their name: a witness afraid of retaliation, a neighbour who can’t be seen talking to police, someone reporting a person close to them,” the statement said. “Their courage has helped solve crimes, prevent tragedies, and save lives. Pausing our program means that option isn’t available now, and we did not make this decision lightly. We are pausing because those people deserve a system we can fully stand behind.” Canadian Crime Stoppers Association and Navigate360 did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Navigate360 told Toronto Crime Stoppers that the stolen data contained 176,859 Toronto tips, which were reported between January 2022 and November 2025, the Toronto chapter’s statement said. The vendor also told Toronto Crime Stoppers that it had found 14,973 names in those tips, but could not say if the names belonged to tipsters, suspects or both. Toronto Crime Stoppers has made “numerous requests” through their lawyers for the text of the stolen tips, but Navigate360 has not responded, the statement said. “Since March, Navigate360 has told us repeatedly that P3 is secure,” the statement said. “In April, it told us Toronto’s data had not been taken. When it told us in June that Toronto’s data was affected, it didn’t say what was exposed.” A hacktivist collective known as Internet Yiff Machine took responsibility for the March breach, saying its goal was to prove that Navigate360 and P3 Global Intel lied about their capabilities. No previous articleNo new articlesSuzanne Smalley is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

1axmx5k.text: Japanese gaming giant Capcom has confirmed that hackers breached its membership service, CAPCOM ID, exposing more than 11.7 million customer email addresses and associated information. Apart from emails, exposed data includes account creation date, last login timestamp, number of logins, and the IP address used at the last login. Capcom found that for a small subset of 43 accounts, dates of birth, gender, nicknames, and countries were also exposed. For another subset of 196 accounts, the hackers changed the CAPCOM ID login passwords in an attempt to lock the owners out, but the company took action and reset them. In an alert today, the gaming company says that passwords for all other registered members have not been exposed and that credit card information remained unaffected. Capcom is a Japanese video game developer and publisher known for franchises such as Resident Evil, Monster Hunter, Street Fighter, and Mega Man. The company has 4,000 employees and an annual revenue of $1.24 billion. CAPCOM ID is the company’s shared account system used for accessing its web services and playing some of its online games. Although the timing of the breach remains unclear, Capcom said it detected suspicious activity and confirmed unauthorized access on October 19. An investigation was launched immediately, and by the following day, it was clear that customer information had been compromised. October 21, the company reported the incident to the police and to Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission. Capcom said its online services remain unaffected, but cautioned users to stay vigilant for unsolicited communications and emails requesting additional information, or messages containing URLs and attachments. During the investigation, Capcom identified the intrusion method and implemented security measures to prevent similar incidents. However, no details related to the initial access have been shared. The gaming firm also says it will notify affected customers in stages, likely due to the large volume of affected accounts, but it has established region-specific communication channels to submit support requests. In November 2020, Capcom suffered an attack claimed by the Ragnar Locker ransomware gang, in which attackers claimed to have stolen 1 TB of data. The company subsequently warned that up to 390,000 people could be affected. In April 2021, Capcom disclosed that the attackers had gained access through an old VPN device. 1ta8iwf.text: Hackers compromised the LiteLLM project’s PyPI package and published malicious Docker images with a payload that steals credentials, secrets, and environment variables. The supply-chain attack affected all PyPI wheels (.whl installation packages) for LiteLLM version 1.107.0, impacting Windows, Linux, and macOS systems. LiteLLM is an open-source Python SDK and AI gateway that enables applications to access AI models from different providers through a common API. It is a massively popular project with 61,800 GitHub stars, 92 million monthly downloads on PyPI, and is used by high-profile companies like NVIDIA, Netflix, AT&T, and Okta. The project says that the release pipeline was compromised on October 21 and a threat actor pushed version 1.107.0 to the Docker registry and PyPI. "This version contained compiled malware which steals credentials and loads remote-code execution tools," the maintainer says, adding that customers running the private enterprise were not impacted. In a post-mortem of the incident, the maintainer says that the following LiteLLM artifacts were affected in the attack: PyPI: litellm==1.107.0: all seven wheels, live from 11:39:51 to 13:23 UTC Docker Hub: v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable: pointed to compromised image index sha256:1bbcb1443bc962e45f5aad53fe3d2c30600e0379715fb6c664cdd3ac126c339e from 11:46:56 to 14:20 UTC GHCR: v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable: pointed to the compromised image indexes below from 11:46:56 UTC until they were made unavailable by 13:51 UTC ghcr.io/berriai/litellm: sha256:1bbcb1443bc9… ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-database: sha256:c00f9d92c427… ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-non_root: sha256:7b00e91cd2fe… Multiple application security companies detected the attack within six minutes of publishing the malicious LiteLLM version and analyzed the payload. According to the researchers, the attacker did not touch the LiteLLM application code and modified only the installation package to place three malicious files (cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py) in the environment's Python’s library directory. "During normal startup, Python processes executable .pth lines and then attempts to import sitecustomize," Socket researchers explain. Endor Labs notes that this way the payloads are executed before the application every time Python is launched in the environment. Running Python or pip to investigate an affected installation also triggered the malware. The malware targeted the following data: Cloud and deployment credentials: AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, Docker, and infrastructure-management secrets. AI credentials and configuration: Authentication files for AI development tools, plus LiteLLM’s stored provider credentials and model settings. Developer secrets and private keys: Git, GitHub, npm, PyPI, and CI/CD credentials; .env files; SSH, GPG, and TLS keys. Browser data: Saved login, cookie, autofill/payment, and browsing-history databases. Host and runtime data: Environment variables, shell and application histories, and system and network information. The stolen data is encrypted using an AES-256-CBC key that is encrypted with an RSA-4096 key and then uploaded to ‘litellm[.]dev/healthcheck’ One of the malicious files, sitecustomize.py, launches a detached loader that checks a GitHub-hosted pointer every hour and downloads Python from an external server for execution on the host. The malicious packages have been removed, but potentially impacted users should stop affected deployments and inspect environments without launching the Python interpreter. Infected systems should be isolated and rebuilt from clean backups, and all exposed secrets should be rotated immediately. Removing the LiteLLM package directory alone may leave startup files or an active loader behind. Currently, the recommended recovery version is LiteLLM 1.106.2, which is the latest clean release before the attack. Previously, the project also suffered a breach in March, when the TeamPCP hacking group published malicious LiteLLM versions on PyPI after breaching Aqua Security's Trivy vulnerability scanner used in LiteLLM's CI/CD pipeline.
