Sure, the model writes the attacks. But everything that makes those attacks safe to run against production and worth acting on afterward lives in the harness around the model. The harness is where the engineering in AI pentesting sits. The Hugging Face intrusion OpenAI disclosed in July showed what happens when that harness gives way, even inside an OpenAI evaluation built to contain the agents. Why Each Control Takes Rigorous Engineering Let’s take a closer look at the attack different stages and the role AI agents can take there Scope A pentesting agent makes thousands of decisions about where to send its next request, and the model judges each one against a rule written in plain language. A web app’s real boundary often extends past one domain through redirects and calls to outside services. Enforcing scope means code that inspects every request before it leaves, and OWASP’s 2026 guidance routes privileged actions through a deterministic policy engine that checks them at execution time, outside the model. Credentials Finding exposed credentials is part of what a pentest does, so the agent regularly comes across working keys outside its assignment. Which of those it may use, for what, and when a person gets involved are policy decisions that the code around the model applies on every attempt. Prompt Injection Every page and API response the agent reads, including hidden fields, metadata and comments a user never sees, can carry content written by anyone who can post to the app. A single product review is enough to plant malicious instructions. OWASP ranks prompt injection the top risk for LLM applications and notes that no reliable prevention exists today. The design question is not whether the model gets fooled, but how much damage it can do if and when it does. That comes down to two things: how tightly each action is constrained and which actions require further inspection and human sign-off. Neither is simple. OWASP warns that approval fatigue degrades reviewer judgement at scale, so routing everything to a human simply shifts the failure point down the line. Proof In October 2026, Google stopped accepting product vulnerability reports to its open-source bug bounty program after a surge in automated submissions, the majority of which it said were not valid. A finding a developer can’t reproduce is just another ticket to close. Producing one worth acting on means running the exploit, capturing what it reached, and packaging the result so anyone can replay it, all within the limits of the other controls set. None of this is built once. Every model upgrade can change how the agent behaves, and every release changes the app whose security it tests. And around the controls sit the systems a production agent depends on, including change-triggered testing, routing findings to the developers who own the code, strictly controlling what customer data reaches a model provider, and connecting what the agent finds in the app to the rest of the environment. Across all of it, the pattern is the same. The model reasons about what to try, and deterministic code decides what runs, records it, and stops it when needed. How Pentera Apps Implements the Harness This separation of reasoning and execution is how we approach building Pentera Apps. Instead of letting an AI model send requests directly into an application, Pentera Apps pairs an AI that decides what to test with a deterministic harness that controls what runs. Every action is logged and any test can be paused or stopped at any time. It's the same safety discipline Pentera has applied to production testing for nearly a decade, across thousands of global customers. The harness also produces the proof. Every finding ships with a replayable exploit script, a CVSS 3.1 score and CWE mapping, so developers can reproduce the attack themselves instead of taking it on trust. Once the fix lands, the exact same attack can be re-run to confirm the path is closed. Tests run on demand or on a schedule, with change-triggered testing in CI/CD coming next, so validation stays inline with development. The surrounding systems follow the same discipline. Only minimal, redacted data reaches the LLM, with zero retention and no training on customer data, and data stays in the customer’s region. Every test starts with context from reconnaissance across the customer’s attack surfaces, findings from their security stack, and live threat intelligence signals. That context lets Pentera trace an exploit in a web app be traced into network, cloud, and identity on one platform. In agentic pentesting, the harness determines the results. Pentera Apps builds it in, so security teams get validated findings without building one themselves. Note: This article has been expertly written and contributed by Assaf Regev, AVP Product Marketing at Pentera. Security teams can sign up for early access to Pentera Apps, Agentic Web App Pentesting.

esygxk.text: Attackers took control of more than 300 Tor exit relays in early October and used them to redirect SSH connections to servers that stole login passwords, a researcher found. Exit relays are the last hop in a Tor circuit, where traffic leaves the network for its destination. Only a password login to an SSH server made through Tor between October 1 and 5, after accepting the interception server's host key, could have been captured. The Tor Project began flagging relays on October 4, and by October 5, none remained in the consensus, the list of relays that Tor clients use. At the peak on October 4, the relays carrying the attacker's exit policy made up 7.46% of Tor's exit capacity, measured by consensus weight, according to an analysis of public Tor directory data posted to the tor-relays mailing list. The researcher, who publishes as kaba, scanned all of Tor's roughly 3,000 exits on October 2 and found 333 redirecting SSH to the same 12 interception servers. The directory-data analysis counts 377 relays run by 59 operators that switched to the attacker's exit policy between October 1 and 4, which it calls "a policy match, not proof of compromise." How the Hijacked Exits Intercepted SSH An exit relay only carries traffic to the ports its exit policy allows. The attackers rewrote that policy in the relays' torrc configuration files to allow port 22 (the SSH port), enabling SSH on 342 relays that had blocked it. Another 24 relays that had not been exits at all became exits. "It seems the attacker is gaining access to Linux based hosts and when these machines are running non-exits they are editing the torrc file and turning them into exits to be able to carry out the SSH attack," the Tor Project's network health team wrote in its October 5 notice to relay operators. Most of the affected relays were already exits, the directory data shows. The same change closed the encrypted mail ports, IMAPS and POP3S, and on most relays opened the plaintext-capable ones, POP3 and IMAP. A Tor client only picks an exit that allows the destination port, so these relays stopped carrying encrypted mail and started carrying SSH, Telnet, and, on most of them, plaintext mail. Why the encrypted mail ports were closed is not visible in the data, the analysis says. With port 22 open, an SSH connection through one of these exits went to one of 12 interception servers instead of its destination, kaba found. When a server intercepted the connection, it presented its own host key. A user who already knew the real server's key saw OpenSSH's warning that the remote host identification had changed, and a user connecting for the first time saw the usual prompt to accept a new key. In the October 2 scan, about a dozen exits were serving a fake host key, and the other 300 or so redirected through the same servers without altering the key. A user who accepted the key and typed a password handed it to the interceptor. The interceptor connected to the real server, so the session worked, and every command could be watched and separately logged in with the stolen password to check for sudo and run a base64-encoded Perl installer. In kaba's honeypot, the installer took the same form as the command that put Ebury, a backdoor that hides inside OpenSSH, on one of a relay operator's servers, as described below. A key-based SSH login could not be relayed this way. Under the SSH authentication protocol, , the client's signature includes an identifier unique to each session, so a signature made for the interceptor's session is useless against the real server. The interceptor could still accept a key login itself and show a fake shell, but it could not reach the real server with it. A password, by contrast, travels inside the encrypted session and can be read by the server at the other end, which here was the interceptor. Who Was Exposed, and What to Do If You Were To be exposed, someone had to connect to an SSH server over Tor between October 1 and the afternoon of October 5, land on one of the hijacked exits, have the connection intercepted rather than passed through, accept the interceptor's host key, and log in with a password. No count of victims exists. If you accepted an unfamiliar or changed host key over Tor in that window, treat the password you typed as stolen, change it, and check that server for the Ebury signs listed below. An OpenSSH client that accepted the key saved it in known_hosts. The server that intercepted kaba's connection used an ED25519 key with the fingerprint SHA256:6baCZCPsl+AfQuujUS81fMEE/C7UeJ+AwjrImqmDB3E, though the other interception servers may have used different keys. How It Was Found and Stopped Kaba encountered the attack on the morning of October 2, when an SSH connection over Tor returned a changed-key warning. He then used exitmap, a scanning tool that the Tor Project's network health team also uses, to open an SSH connection from one of his servers to another via each exit in turn. One end checked whether the host key was correct, and the other whether the connection originated at the exit or from an interception server. He reported the results to the health team that evening. The health team also spotted the policy change through its own monitoring. On October 4, it contacted Zimmer, who ran the Quetzalcoatl relay family, the largest group of affected relays, and Zimmer confirmed the change was not his, asked for the relays to be marked bad, and stopped Tor on the server running them. Directory authorities began voting the BadExit and MiddleOnly flags on affected relays at 18:00 UTC that day, and the flags were in the consensus by 21:00. BadExit tells Tor clients never to use a relay as an exit. On the morning of October 5,, a scripted restart swept through 55 of Quetzalcoatl's hosts, with the policy still in place. Who ran it is not known. The directory authorities were by then rejecting affected relays from the network, the Tor Project said in its notice, and the two relays Zimmer had stopped were refused when they tried to rejoin, he wrote. By 17:00 UTC on October 5, no relay with the attacker's policy was in the consensus, and none had returned as of October 9, the directory-data analysis found. Forty-one relays, nine of them Quetzalcoatl's, were still publishing the policy at that point but were not listed. Tor Metrics' count of relays carrying the Exit flag fell by about 370 between October 3 and October 5, matching the number of affected relays, and had not recovered by October 18. Ebury, and How the Attackers Got In Zimmer described his side in a post-mortem on the list on October 7. Two of his servers were running Ebury version 1.8.3: a management server at Contabo that served as the family's VPN gateway and SSH jump host, and a FranTech VPS he calls Switzerland2 that ran two of the exits. Ebury is a backdoor and credential stealer for OpenSSH that has been active since 2009, according to ESET, which estimated in 2024 that it had infected 400,000 servers, with more than 100,000 still infected in late 2023. The attacker logged in to the management server on August 28 with the operator account's password on the first try, gained root within five minutes, installed Ebury, then reached Switzerland2 a little over an hour later and installed it there too. "The root cause was ours: one password reused for SSH login, sudo and the backup passphrase, stored in plaintext on both servers, plus SSH password authentication left enabled on the internet-facing management server," Zimmer wrote. Where the attacker got that password is unknown. Ebury's backdoor logins leave no record. On October 2, the exits' configuration files were rewritten with no login, sudo command, or cron job in the logs, and the two relays published the attacker's policy at 09:34 UTC. It stayed live for about 52 hours on two relays moving roughly 3.4 TiB a day. A routine reboot on October 4 killed the attacker's hidden tools, but Ebury came straight back. The family's "offline" master keys "were not offline: copies sat in the workstation backup on the management server, encrypted with the password the attacker already had," Zimmer wrote. He retired every relay and the bridge in the family and deleted both servers. This Ebury is a single setuid library file, /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libkeyutils.so.1.10.2, with the libkeyutils.so.1 symlink pointed at it. The packaged library is untouched, so dpkg -V and debsums do not catch it, and sshd, sudo, and PAM pass their package checks. Version 1.8.3 is newer than ESET's public indicators, which stop at 1.8.2, and ESET's published detection script, read on October 21, lists no socket name for it. Marc-Etienne M. Léveillé, who co-wrote ESET's 2014 Ebury paper, wrote its 2024 report and has since left the company, replied that version 1.8.3 has been around since at least June 2026 and posted an updated copy of the script that covers it. "Given how many servers had Ebury between 2009 and 2023 (400 000!), there are most likely other compromised Tor relays out there," he wrote. How the other 58 operators' hosts were entered is the main open question. Among their relays listed on October 1, 71 of the 101 hosted on FranTech Solutions, the network behind the BuyVM hosting brand, switched to the attacker's policy, against 13 of 9,054 hosted elsewhere, the directory-data analysis found. Forty relays of 21 operators changed within five and a half minutes on October 1, most by a configuration reload, which the analysis reads as one actor already holding access to all 40. Léveillé's best guess for the password was a login from a host already running Ebury, with a compromised hosting provider as another possibility. ESET has seen providers whose management servers ran Ebury and whose customers' virtual servers ended up infected, he wrote. Kaba counted 26 of the 27 compromised servers outside the Quetzalcoatl family at FranTech/BuyVM and asked on the list: "Could they have compromised those servers at the hoster level?" Quetzalcoatl's own compromise ran through its Contabo management server, and 225 of its 273 affected relays sat on other networks. Who is behind the campaign is unknown, and so is how many of the affected hosts ran Ebury: Zimmer examined two of his, and the directory data shows only the policy. A fake uppercase CRON daemon and NAT rules redirecting port 22 were among the signs other operators reported to the Tor Project. Zimmer's servers had neither, and whether the cases share one actor is open. On Zimmer's relays, the port changes meant any mail retrieval could only happen in plaintext, he wrote, and a hidden process named snf ran on Switzerland2 for most of the window. What it did is unknown. What Relay Operators Should Check The Tor Project's notice asks Linux relay operators to check Relay Search for an Exit flag or exit policy they did not set, and to look through torrc and any included files for changed ExitRelay, ExitPolicy, ContactInfo, MyFamily or Nickname lines. It also lists NAT rules on port 22, unknown listening processes or outbound connections, new users, authorized_keys entries, cron jobs and systemd units, and a tor binary that fails its package check. Zimmer's servers showed none of the host-level signs on that list, only the changed exit policy, so a clean host check does not rule out this Ebury. The signs of the implant, from Zimmer's post, are: File: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libkeyutils.so.1.10.2, setuid and owned by no package (63,368 bytes on his servers, with a hash that differs on every server) Symlink: libkeyutils.so.1 pointing at that file Socket: abstract UNIX socket @event-0YsOG9WSOE Process: a fake /sbin/rsyslogd (earlier systemd-udevd or arpd) running inside the ssh.service cgroup IP: 185.225.226[.]62, the source of the August 28 login SSH key: RSA SHA256:dvACokMYcXJ2om4wuS+TvdtjrAgPK7rC7ZQHDgvBHzk, used to log in to Switzerland2 SSH keys embedded in the implant: RSA SHA256:KlICz/B59619CpuQdGzgmmvzWBfTMUJ77EwihTYobuo and ED25519 SHA256:OfLY0uF9SwOW9xVjiMXZGDfk6Atmz6CbHy4epknLm8Y Interceptor host key: ED25519 SHA256:6baCZCPsl+AfQuujUS81fMEE/C7UeJ+AwjrImqmDB3E, seen on kaba's connection Check from a rescue system or an offline disk image if you can. On a live server, log in with a key. "Never type a password into a server you suspect, because Ebury will capture it," Zimmer wrote. Start a shell with H=1 I=1 LD_PRELOAD=":" LD_DEBUG=":" bash to get past the userland rootkit before running Léveillé's updated script or the commands in Zimmer's post. If you find it, the Tor Project's steps are: take the relay offline preserve the disk and logs before wiping reinstall rather than clean up generate a new relay identity and treat the old keys as stolen rotate every credential that was on the host Reinstalling matters because the implant survived a reboot on Zimmer's server. Report to bad-relays@lists.torproject.org, and if your IP address was blocked during the incident, write to the same address once your host is clean to have the block lifted, Georg Koppen of the Tor Project said in a follow-up.

8we56b.text: This story is developing and was written before PHP's scheduled 14:00 UTC release on October 21. Once the release is out, the affected and fixed versions below are confirmed by the official advisory. PHP will ship an out-of-cycle security release at 14:00 UTC today, October 21, for two critical vulnerabilities that its security team has rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 scale but has not described. Security researchers at watchTowr say the two flaws allow remote code execution. Only the four supported PHP branches, 8.2 through 8.5, can receive the fix, and no exploitation has been reported so far. The advance notice followed a leak. On October 20, a post on HN said two PHP remote code execution flaws, rated CVSS 10.0 and affecting versions from PHP 5 onward, would be disclosed on Thursday, October 22. The poster said they had "no evidence beyond 'source: trust me, bro'". watchTowr then posted on X that the leaked information was real, that the two flaws were under embargo, that everyone had been supposed to wait until Thursday, and that it could not share more for now. PHP published its notice that evening, at 19:33 UTC, with the release set for Wednesday, a day before the date watchTowr gave. The notice says PHP may release earlier "should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild." The leak carried the flaws' existence, a score, a date, and two CVE identifiers, not how the flaws work. The CVSS 10.0 figure is the leak's. PHP's rating is 9.2 on version 4.0 of the scale. The identifiers researchers are using, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, were also listed in the leaked post. PHP's notice names neither. The claim that every version since PHP 5 is affected is unconfirmed too: watchTowr's own FAQ on the flaws says that scope "has not been confirmed by an official vendor advisory" and that no configuration or feature requirement has been described. PHP says "Full details, affected versions, and the fixed versions will be published with the release." Researchers have started calling the pair php2shell. The name is theirs, not PHP's. Whatever the affected range turns out to be, PHP issues fixes only for its four supported branches, and records each branch's changes in its changelog. Versions 8.2 and 8.3 receive only security fixes, and 8.4 and 8.5 are in active support. Ahead of the release, several trackers, including Alpine Linux's and security researcher Kevin Beaumont, expect the fixes to ship as PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, the next point release of each branch, though PHP has not confirmed the numbers. Anything older, including 8.1, 8.0, 7.x, and 5.x, is end of life and gets no PHP fix. If the flaws reach those branches, installations on them will have no vendor patch. PHP branches that can receive today's fix Branch Current release (September 24) PHP support status 8.5 8.5.11 Active support until December 31, 2027 8.4 8.4.26 Active support until December 31, 2026 8.3 8.3.35 Security fixes only until December 31, 2027 8.2 8.2.34 Security fixes only until December 31, 2026 Security company Mallory counted about 884,000 internet-facing hosts whose HTTP banner reported a PHP version of 8.1 or older to the Shodan search engine on October 20, 59% of the roughly 1.5 million hosts that reported any version. The count covers banners, not confirmed affected systems, and a further 740,000 hosts reported PHP without a version. PHP has published no workaround. Until the release lands, the preparation comes down to six steps, most of them drawn from a rapid-response post from Huntress, with CERT-EU's isolation advice added. Inventory every PHP install, including PHP bundled in vendor appliances, Windows software, and control panels such as cPanel and Plesk. Be ready to upgrade at 14:00 UTC. Patch internet-facing systems first, and check your Linux distribution and hosting provider for backported packages. On an end-of-life branch, upgrade, take the system off the internet, or put it behind a VPN or a web application firewall until you can. Where patching cannot be done at once, CERT-EU advises that you "consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix is available." Watch what PHP starts. Alert on php-fpm, php-cgi, httpd, or apache2 launching shells, interpreters, or download tools. On Linux servers without endpoint detection, Florian Roth's process-watcher logs every program a PHP process starts, with its command line. It sees a program only after it has started and, in Roth's words, "prevents nothing." If you find something, isolate the server, preserve the web server and PHP logs, and look for web shells, new files in the web root, new cron jobs, scheduled tasks, and accounts. Huntress said it had not seen exploitation of the flaws in its partner environments as of October 20, had not built or reproduced a proof of concept, and was not aware of public exploit code. watchTowr's FAQ lists exploitation as none reported as of October 21 and the flaws as not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. For comparison, when CVE-2024-4577, a PHP flaw in CGI mode on Windows, became public in June 2024, Akamai saw exploit attempts against its honeypot servers within 24 hours. The release should clarify what the notice withheld: which versions are affected, which part of PHP is involved, whether an attack requires a particular way of running PHP, a configuration, or a login, and how PHP itself describes the flaws. At the time of writing, PHP had not released the fixes.

e4cdag.text: Unknown threat actors breached TeamUpdraft's website and potentially gained unauthorized access to customers' connection keys for UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault, and UpdraftClone, using them to backdoor WordPress sites. TeamUpdraft is the developer behind UpdraftPlus, a popular WordPress backup plugin with over four million active installations. The vendor also offers UpdraftCentral, a remote management service that's used for managing multiple sites remotely. A client component of UpdraftCentral is shipped within every copy of UpdraftPlus. "Over the weekend of 17-18 October we identified unauthorized access to the teamupdraft.com website," TeamUpdraft said in a statement. "Our team responded straight away and worked through the night to contain it – we closed the access route, signed out every account and replaced the keys and credentials that could have been affected." As a result of the incident, threat actors are believed to have accessed its customer database, which holds the following information - Names, email addresses, billing addresses and order history Account passwords, stored only in hashed (scrambled) form and never in plain text Two-factor authentication (2FA) settings Connection keys for UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault and UpdraftClone TeamUpdraft said the database does not hold any financial information, and that they are handled by Stripe and PayPal. It also emphasized that the UpdraftPlus plugin, along with self-hosted versions of UpdraftCentral and backups sent to customers' own remote storage, are not impacted. "However, if your site was accessed through UpdraftCentral, please also re-authorise your remote storage and change any storage access keys, as a precaution," it said. In addition, TeamUpdraft said it deployed a fix to address the underlying issue, signed out every teamupdraft.com account and reset login security across the site, and released UpdraftPlus 1.26.13 (free) and 2.26.13 (Premium) to automatically disconnect every UpdraftCentral connection made before 10 p.m. BST on October 18, 2026, to prevent the old keys from working. Other steps taken by the developer are listed below - Disconnected every site from UpdraftVault and issued new credentials Replaced every UpdraftClone client key Rotated its keys with payment providers and other connected services Implemented additional monitoring in place Reported the incident to the U.K. Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and other relevant authorities Users who have a teamupdraft.com account are advised to change their password with immediate effect (and elsewhere, if the same password has been reused), reset 2FA settings, and exercise caution when receiving unexpected emails claiming to be from TeamUpdraft. TeamUpdraft is also recommending that cloud customers of UpdraftCentral follow the steps below as soon as possible, since the connection keys can send commands to the connected sites - Log in to the site's own WordPress dashboard, not through UpdraftCentral. Update UpdraftPlus to version 1.26.12 (free) or 2.26.12 (Premium) or later. Disconnect it from UpdraftCentral: go to Settings > UpdraftPlus > Advanced Tools > UpdraftCentral and delete the connection key. Go to Users and check for any administrator accounts you don’t recognise. Remove them. Go to Plugins, including the Must-Use tab if you can see it, and check for anything you don’t recognise. Remove it. Change the passwords for all administrator accounts on the site. If you find anything suspicious, consider restoring the site from a backup taken before 17 October. Reconnect the site to UpdraftCentral. UpdraftVault users are being urged to reconnect their sites to the backup service, and UpdraftClone users who have created a client key are required to copy the new keys from My Account > UpdraftClone > UpdraftClone Key Management and share them with their clients. The development comes as WordPress security company Patchstack said it observed an attacker holding valid UpdraftCentral dashboard keys issuing commands to install backdoor plugins on connected WordPress sites. The campaign is said to have run continuously through an 18-hour window on October 18 and 19, 2026. "The attacker sends a signed plugin.upload_plugin command over the plugin's remote procedure call channel, which listens on ordinary POST requests to the site root. WordPress installs and activates the supplied plugin through its standard installer," Patchstack security researcher Dave Jong said. Slovakia-based penetration testing company Nethemba, which first detected the attack in the wild, has described the rogue plugin as a backdoor that hooks into every request to the site to check if the URL contains the parameter "?_9f5696=" and compares it with a 32-character token. If a matching token is detected, it creates a user "data-ops43" with the display name "Site Tools," assigns it the Editor role, and grants the account "manage_options" and "install_plugins" permissions, allowing the operator to upload arbitrary PHP plugins and open site settings. "Enabling registration and setting the default role to administrator is enough for the attacker to create a full administrator," Nethemba said. "On a standard WordPress site, an Editor also has unfiltered_html, so the account can put JavaScript into posts that runs in the browser of every administrator." "The backdoor has a second layer as well. The account it creates, with a known password, stays in WordPress even after the plugin is removed, and the attacker can log in with it through the normal login form unless two-factor authentication is enabled for that account." Although an early version of the plugin suffered from a coding error that causes impacted sites to fail with error 500, Nethemba said the threat actor deleted the broken backdoor by sending a "plugin.delete_plugin" command and then uploaded a working version that creates a full administrator account or logs in as an existing administrator. WordPress site owners are advised to check for the following indicators of compromise - Plugin names: Site Health Cache or Site Health 364F, Asset Forge 2, Content Helper, Wp Forge, Query Shelf, Style Bridge 8F5, Media Kit 183, Query Shelf, Post Dock 776, Nav Hub, Speed Desk, Speed Kit 300, Link Latch, Script Shelf, or Feed Case Account names: system_team850, web.tech988, cmseditor170, cms.tech644 or web_mgr684, with an email at @example.com and a display name such as System Team, Web Tech, System Staff, System Ops, or Cms Tech IP addresses: 43.250.53.42 and 2a09:bac5:4e21:2e3c::49b:9 In all, Patchstack said it observed 99 distinct backdoor plugin names, with each sample carrying the line "Small maintenance toolkit: keeps option storage tidy." Wordfence, which published its own analysis of the incident, said a WordPress site may be affected if the below criteria are satisfied - The site had UpdraftPlus Free or UpdraftPlus Premium installed and active while the affected UpdraftCentral connection key was present. The site has, or had during the incident, an active connection key for TeamUpdraft’s cloud-hosted UpdraftCentral service. "This is the second incident in this channel in five months," Patchstack warned. "In June 2026 the vendor fixed CVE-2026-10795 (CVSS 8.1), where an obsolete unsigned message format let an attacker forge UpdraftCentral commands with no keys at all. That was fixed in 1.26.5 and 2.26.5, but exploitation attempts continue, so sites below those versions face both problems at once." The development comes days after the website of the Rank Math PRO WordPress plugin was hit by a software supply chain attack, causing users who downloaded version 3.0.123 between October 15 at 8:02 p.m. UTC and October 16 at 7:12 a.m. UTC to receive compromised versions that planted hidden backdoors. The incident has been assigned the CVE identifier CVE-2026-111862 (CVSS score: 9.8). The issue was fixed in Rank Math PRO version 3.0.124. "The malware may establish persistent access, communicate with rank1cdn[.]com, recreate hidden backdoors on page visits, and expose WordPress credentials, database credentials, API keys, and other secrets accessible to the web server," Wordefence said. The findings also coincide with an advisory from PHP, which said it intends to ship a security release that fixes two critical vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, CVSS scores: 9.2), as information about the flaws leaked ahead of their scheduled disclosure. The flaws have been codenamed PHP2Shell. According to watchTowr CEO Benjamin Harris, the vulnerabilities affect PHP versions 5, 6, 7, and 8, and were originally due for release on October 22 at 11 a.m. ET. "PHP is everywhere. It quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," Huntress said. "When a critical bug lands in PHP itself, rather than in one app built on top of it, the number of places you have to go looking to identify vulnerable PHP versions gets very big, very fast."

izorrv.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 21, 2026Artificial Intelligence / National Security U.S. federal civilian agencies must remove DeepSeek products from their information technology systems, along with any third-party products or services "developed using DeepSeek implementations," under a Department of Homeland Security order. They may also no longer buy information technology products or services from the Chinese AI developer or its affiliates Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin issued the order, dated July 24, 2026, under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018, and the department published it in the Federal Register on October 20. The notice does not define "DeepSeek implementations." The order names Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd., the developer of the R1 and V3 models, and covers its affiliates as defined in federal acquisition rules. The company's privacy policy says it collects, processes and stores users' personal data in the People's Republic of China. Under the 2018 law, the Federal Acquisition Security Council recommends exclusion and removal orders, and three officials may issue them: the Secretary of Homeland Security for civilian agencies, the Secretary of Defense for the Defense Department and national security systems, and the Director of National Intelligence for the intelligence community. The DeepSeek order therefore covers only what civilian agencies buy and run. It does not restrict companies or the public. The 2018 law was first used in 2025, when the Director of National Intelligence excluded Acronis, a Swiss cybersecurity and data protection company, from intelligence community procurement and ordered its products removed from intelligence community systems. Executive agencies "shall comply with exclusion and removal orders," the law says. An agency can ask the official who issued an order for an exception, and under the council's regulations the request must be in writing and give a compelling justification. DHS directs questions about the order to CISA's FASCSA Order Implementation Team at fascsa.orders@cisa.dhs.gov. The order also reaches government contractors. A federal contract that carries FAR clause 52.204-30 bars the contractor from providing or using, in performing the contract, any product or service covered by an applicable FASCSA order, unless the issuing official has granted a waiver. The clause also requires the contractor to: Search SAM.gov for the phrase "FASCSA order" at least once every three months Make a reasonable inquiry into its supply chain when a new order could affect it Report any covered product or service it has provided or used to the contracting officer within 3 business days of identifying it Send further information on mitigation within 10 business days of that report Include the clause in its subcontracts An order issued after a solicitation applies to an existing contract only once the contracting officer adds it by amendment or modification. The Federal Register notice gives no reasons for the order. The signed order is attached to the notice as four scanned pages and is posted on regulations.gov under docket DHS-2026-0628. The order is dated July 24. DHS filed it for public inspection at the Federal Register on October 19, 87 days later, and it was published the next day. The council's regulations leave public release of an order to the issuing official, who "May provide a copy of the order to other persons, including through public disclosure." They set no deadline for it. The law requires the issuing official to notify the company named in an order and the appropriate congressional committees, and to review the order at least once a year. Before the order, U.S. restrictions on DeepSeek were device bans adopted one body at a time. By February 2025, Congress, NASA, the Navy, the Pentagon and Texas had barred DeepSeek from government devices. Bills to bar DeepSeek on government devices were introduced in the House and Senate that month and had not advanced past committee as of October 21. China's foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a briefing on October 20 that "China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security" and that Beijing will "resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies," the Associated Press reported. DeepSeek did not immediately respond to the AP's request for comment.

19xps75.text: State Bank of India has identified 3,897 customer records containing personal information in a set of about 375,000 records available on the dark web, and it does not yet know where the data came from. The state-owned bank, India's largest, said in a stock-exchange filing dated October 21 that it "has experienced an incident involving the loss of certain data." The count is preliminary, and the bank has yet to establish whether the data is authentic, how far the exposure goes and what risk it poses to customers. The exposed information "reportedly included customers' registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, gender, email addresses, residential addresses, branch and CIF identifiers, lead IDs, and metadata associated with loan/lead records and other related files," in the filing's words. A CIF identifier is the customer information file number, the bank's internal ID for each customer. The bank has not said whether the 3,897 records belong to 3,897 different people, or what the rest of the set contains. The 3,897 are roughly 1 in 100 of the records it examined. Account numbers, balances, passwords, one-time passcodes, card details and government identity numbers such as PAN or Aadhaar are not among the categories the filing lists. The risk in the listed categories is impersonation: a caller or message that uses a customer's name, mobile number, date of birth, address, branch, and internal ID to appear to come from the bank. The alert reached the bank on October 16 via its threat intelligence provider, CERT-In, India's national computer emergency response team, and the Defense Cyber Agency, the armed forces' cyber agency under the Ministry of Defense. The bank activated its incident response and containment procedures and engaged an independent cybersecurity firm from CERT-In's panel of approved security auditors to assess what the filing calls "the alleged compromise." The incident has no material impact on the bank's core business operations, financial performance or business continuity, the filing says. That covers the bank's business, not its customers. The filing names no attacker, forum or dataset. The figure of about 375,000 matches a claim that the monitoring account CyberPulse56 flagged on X on October 16. The account said a threat actor using the name Siriusim claimed to have leaked customer documents and personal data linked to SBI: 375,000 rows in CSV format and 2,722 PDF documents, said to include personal information, loan applications and supporting documents, account-opening forms and addresses. The Free Press Journal examined the listing on BreachForums, a cybercrime forum used to trade stolen data, and found 4 sample records posted with the listing. The phone numbers in the samples were valid. The WhatsApp profile picture on one number matched the passport-size photograph on that person's KYC document, which the actor had also posted. That check covers 4 records and does not show that the whole set is genuine or where it came from. The samples were mostly loan-related and carried KYC fields, and they did not show whether the data belonged to SBI itself, one of its subsidiaries, or a third-party provider that handles banking applications. Nothing in the bank's filing ties its analysis to the listing, and the bank has not said whether the 2,722 PDF documents were part of what it examined. Whether any SBI system was breached is an open question. The filing leaves the source of the data to the investigation and gives no date for when the data first appeared. The filing does not mention whether affected customers have been or will be told. The bank's cyber security page, last updated in June, tells customers to report any cyber incident to report.phishing@sbi.co.in or the national cybercrime helpline, 1930. That is general advice, written before the incident. Bank of Baroda, another state-owned bank, told the exchanges on July 27 about a cyber-security incident in nearly the same words, including "the alleged compromise," after receiving "a communication from an anonymous source claiming access to certain data." That filing named a preliminary cause, "potential business email compromise." SBI's names none.

o1e1zt.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 21, 2026Vulnerability / Malware The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added four vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, including four vulnerabilities impacting Plex Media Server that's collectively called Plex2Shell. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-96652 (CVSS score: 5.3) - Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability CVE-2026-96654 (CVSS score: 6.9) - Plex Media Server improper neutralization of encoded URI schemes in a web page Vulnerability CVE-2026-96655 (CVSS score: 5.3) - Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability CVE-2026-96656 (CVSS score: 8.6) - Plex Media Server external control of file name or path Vulnerability According to security researcher Zach Main, who discovered and reported the vulnerabilities, a remote attacker could chain the four vulnerabilities to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution. The issues were addressed in Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861 released on August 3, 2026. The addition of the four vulnerabilities to the KEV catalog follows a report from security researcher boredhackerblog, who found that threat actors are weaponizing the flaws to deploy cryptocurrency miners and proxy malware. CISA has also flagged two other vulnerabilities as actively exploited. One of them is a DLL sideloading vulnerability in Siemens Software Center (CVE-2026-110936, CVSS score: 8.4) that has been abused in ClickFix attacks using a platform called Romulus. The second security flaw is a command injection bug in EG Secure Solutions SiteGuard Server Edition (CVE-2026-106931, CVSS score: 8.5) that the Japanese company confirmed as being exploited. No additional details related to the exploitation activity are currently available. CISA is urging Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to apply fixes for CVE-2026-106931, CVE-2026-96656, and CVE-2026-96654 by October 23, 2026, and the rest by November 3, 2026.

1ah7igo.text: A Belarus-aligned hacktivist group spent nearly two years within the network of a Russian healthcare organization. According to a report published by Russian cybersecurity firm Solar, the activity has been attributed to a threat cluster dubbed Partisan Zmiy, which is also known as the Cyber Partisans. Known to be active since at least 2020, the group has a track record of striking industrial enterprises and government agencies in Russia and Belarus with a backdoor called Vasilek that uses Telegram for command-and-control (C2) and data exfiltration. Some of the attacks have also leveraged phishing lures to deliver an installer that simultaneously deploys the legitimate FortiClient VPN program on the system as well as an open-source program known as DNSCat2 that allows attackers to gain control of the infected host. A notable aspect of the threat actor is their ability to stage destructive attacks with a wiper referred to as Pryanik, alongside taking steps to systematically clear Windows event logs using a utility dubbed Evlx. The Rostelecom subsidiary said it discovered the intrusion in December 2025, although evidence suggests that the earliest signs of compromise date back to early 2024. The name of the targeted organization was not identified. The exact initial access vector used to breach the entity is also not known. Unlike other attacks linked to Cyber Partisans, the threat actors remained on the network for an extended period of time without carrying out any destructive activity, marking something of a shift in modus operandi. "The attacked organization possessed an extensive infrastructure and two-way trusted relationships with numerous subsidiary medical institutions," Solar said. "We hypothesize that the lack of infrastructure disruption is due precisely to the value of this access for further espionage and trusted relationship attacks." Observed as part of the intrusion is a loader-scheduler service ("vmauad") that masquerades as a legitimate VMware component to maintain persistence and evade cursory inspection. To accomplish this, the attackers are said to have taken advantage of a trusted-but-unmonitored VMware Tools directory location to plant malicious executables or replace legitimate VMware DLLs with a malicious version ("vmtools.dll") containing the backdoor. The primary responsibility of the Windows service is to launch the rogue binary "C:\Program Files\VMware\VMware Tools\authd.exe" that, besides launching a GOST tunnel every Saturday from 10 p.m. to 11 p.m., runs an updated version of Vasilek (version 1.5.8) once, eight hours after the service begins. Once installed, Vasilek is equipped to collect information about an infected computer, execute Windows commands, launch and terminate processes, transfer files, capture screenshots, record keystrokes, and escalate privileges via runas. It can also prevent the machine from going into sleep mode, and update or remove itself. One new addition is the "move_cursor" command that, as the name implies, allows the backdoor to move the cursor and simulate user input on the victim's screen. "The group consistently invests in stealth and operational security, rather than new capabilities: hostname binding in two independent components, nightly scheduled payload launches, system proxy inheritance, disguise as legitimately installed but unused software, file rotation across the same paths, time-stomping, outgoing message suppression, and anonymous messages on behalf of the group in operator chats," Solar said. "The backdoor's feature set has remained largely unchanged over four revisions. Due to Telegram being blocked in Russia by ISPs, communication between the Vasilek backdoor and C2 has become unstable." The disclosure comes as Solar also disclosed details of a phishing campaign that employs JavaScript attachments mimicking business-themed documents, such as payments and purchase orders, to deliver a previously unreported malware family known as HypeAgent. The Windows malware is a full-featured trojan designed to take complete control over infected systems, packing the ability to steal files, open a console, change desktop wallpaper, turn on a webcam, log keystrokes, launch hidden VNC and RDP sessions, control the mouse, and even deploy a cryptocurrency miner. It's also capable of stealing cookies associated with Discord, Steam, GitHub, Instagram, Telegram, Binance, ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor, and tampering with the installed Exodus wallet app to inject JavaScript that can collect the victim's password, PIN, mnemonic phrase, and private key. Earlier this June, Solar also observed legitimate infrastructure compromised by the ProxyCB proxyware botnet malware making automated requests to Russian websites and online platforms, while identifying possible overlaps between the botnet infrastructure and historical activity linked to TeamSpy, a threat cluster known for abusing TeamViewer to facilitate reconnaissance and data theft. Last month, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) charged Searzhudin Tamirlanovich Aktulaev, a 40-year-old Russian national extradited from Cyprus in May 2025, for exploiting an online messaging service of a well-known freelance employment platform to send malware-laced Excel attachments to about 80,000 of its users in 2016 and 2017 using 255 fake accounts. The attacks led to the deployment of two types of malware, a variant of the TVRAT (aka Sheldor, SpyAgent, TeamBot, TeamSpy, and TVSPY) and DarkVNC, to harvest and send data from a victim computer to a remote server under the attacker's control. Thousands of computers are assessed to have been infected as a result of this scheme.

xtc7pt.text: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority (CA) certificates are compromised, Mozilla and Google's Chrome Root Program confirms on October 20. An intermediate CA signs the certificates that websites present, so anyone holding one of these keys could issue a certificate for any website that a browser would accept. A researcher reported the compromise to the root programs on the evening of October 17, and Chrome and Firefox blocked the eight certificates within hours, after Chrome verified the findings. No TLS certificate chaining to the six intermediates used for websites had been logged to Certificate Transparency (CT) before Chrome's block, so none could have been trusted by default in Chrome or any other browser that requires CT logging, the Chrome Root Program said. It is not known how the keys left eMudhra, when, or whether anyone besides the researcher holds them. The keys are the ones Go blocked in its October 20 security releases without naming the CA, as The Hacker News reported earlier. The eight hash values in Go's code match the eight certificates. Go handled the fix on its URGENT track, which its security policy reserves for threats to the ecosystem's integrity or flaws being exploited in the wild, and neither the issue nor the release notes say which applied. What Was Compromised eMudhra is an Indian CA that sells certificates under the emSign brand through companies in India, the United States, and the Netherlands, and it has roots in the Mozilla, Chrome, and Apple root stores. The eight compromised certificates are: TLS, domain validated: EM DV TLS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV, Netherlands) and EM DV TLS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc, United States) TLS, organization validated: EM OV TLS CA - G3B and EM OV TLS CA - G3C TLS, extended validation: EM EV TLS CA - G3B and EM EV TLS CA - G3C Code signing: EM OV CS CA - G3B and EM OV CS CA - G3C The six TLS certificates were issued by emSign Root TLS CA - G3 and chain to emSign ECC Root CA - G3, a root in the Chrome and Apple stores and, until October 20, in Mozilla's. Each of the eight also exists as a second certificate with the same public key, cross-signed by Sectigo under its AAA Certificate Services root, according to a certificate list published by Dennis Jackson, a Mozilla cryptography engineer. Chrome did not need to block the two code-signing certificates, because its TLS verifier will not build a path through an intermediate restricted to code signing, the Chrome Root Program said. Who Is Protected, and How The Chrome Root Program received the report at 18:05 UTC on October 17 and had a CRLSet update blocking the six TLS intermediates in place by 19:45 UTC. Mozilla received it at 20:06 UTC and finished pushing a OneCRL block to Firefox installations with standard settings at 22:59 UTC. CRLSets and OneCRL are revocation lists that the two browsers fetch on their own, so neither needed an update or a restart. Chrome's block matches the public key rather than the certificate, so it also catches the Sectigo cross-signed copies. It is the same mechanism Chrome used earlier this month against rogue certificates for Google domains. The researcher, credited by Mozilla only as Wayne, signed the message "We have a problem here - Wayne" with each of the eight keys and sent it to the root programs that day, according to Jackson, who published the signatures and certificates on a one-page site. eMudhra has revoked the eight certificates. Apple blocked them on October 19, Microsoft on October 20, and other trust stores were notified on October 19, according to Jackson's site. The cross-signed copies did not widen the risk in Chrome or Firefox. Both stopped trusting Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services root for websites in April 2025, and Chrome's root store file does not carry it. Apple's root list for iOS 26 and macOS 26, published in December 2025, includes it. Mozilla does not believe, for now, that the problem affects other CAs, Jackson wrote on Mozilla's policy list, and Chrome said it checked every other CA certificate in its store and "found no other instances of this failure mode." What to Update Browsers get revocation pushed to them. Many other programs that check TLS certificates, from Go binaries to anything using Python's certifi bundle, do not check revocation data and keep trusting a chain until their code or their root bundle changes. Mozilla's advice to anyone who runs a trust store: nothing is needed where clients reliably check revocation and refuse connections when they cannot check, the eight intermediates should be blocked now where the software can block individual intermediates; and otherwise the operator should consider removing trust in the roots that signed them. The fixes published so far, and what each one does: add border: Software Fixed in What it does Status Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 Rejects any chain containing one of the eight keys (CVE-2026-111943) Released October 20, rebuild required Firefox 158.0.1 , ESR 115.43.1 and ESR 153.5.1 Carries the OneCRL block for installations that cannot receive Remote Settings ( CVE-2026-113470 ) Released October 20 NSS 3.131.1 Removes emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from the trusted list Released October 20 Python certifi 2026.10.19 Drops emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from the bundle Released Rust webpki-roots 1.0.10 Drops emSign ECC Root CA - G3 Released Homebrew ca-certificates 2026-09-25_1 Excludes emSign ECC Root CA - G3, emSign Root TLS CA - G3 and AAA Certificate Services by public key Released Node.js None yet A draft change would block the eight keys Pending Composer ca-bundle None yet An open change would remove emSign ECC Root CA - G3 Pending Go's filter sits in the standard library and rejects any chain containing one of the eight keys, on Go's own verifier and on the macOS and Windows system-verifier paths, and the change adds no setting to turn it off. A program picks it up only when rebuilt with the new release; Go 1.25 and older are out of support and get no fixes. Three of the fixes work by removing roots rather than blocking the keys. certifi, webpki-roots, and Homebrew's ca-certificates drop emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from their bundles, and Homebrew also drops Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services root and emSign Root TLS CA - G3. That also cuts off every legitimate certificate that chains to those roots. Mozilla, which made the same change to NSS, said some servers will become unavailable to non-Firefox users of its trust list until those servers move to new certificate chains. Firefox needs nothing unless Remote Settings is disabled by policy or blocked on the network. The October 20 releases carry the block list for those installations. None of the sources provide a way to detect past misuse of the keys beyond Chrome's CT search, which covers only logged certificates. What Happens to eMudhra Mozilla removed emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from NSS on October 20. Chrome will remove the same root in version 43 of its root store and is reviewing the status of eMudhra's other root in its store, emSign Root CA - G1, the Chrome Root Program said, citing the seriousness of the incident. How the keys left eMudhra and when remain open questions. Mozilla said it is working with the CA, other root programs and downstream trust stores on the root cause and will post more when it can. eMudhra's trust-services repository carried no notice about the incident as of October 20. Go has not named the CA on its issue, where its release notes cite "specific security concerns around their operation", and a commenter asked for the hashes in the patch to be explained. Filippo Valsorda, who maintains the cryptography packages in Go's standard library, replied that the keys are compromised and the certificates revoked, that Linux root stores are too poorly maintained for revocation to reach applications, and that putting the keys in code is the only option for now.

1rlr7pt.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 20, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security Cybersecurity researchers have released a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for a recently patched critical security flaw impacting Fortinet FortiSIEM that could result in arbitrary code execution. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-106173 (CVSS score: 9.4), is a critical path traversal flaw that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute unauthorized code or commands via specially crafted packets. Patches for the flaw were released last week by Fortinet in the following versions - FortiSIEM 7.5.0 (Upgrade to 7.5.1 or above) FortiSIEM 7.6 (Not affected) According to Horizon3.ai, the issue involves an unauthenticated attacker connecting to the gRPC service listening on TCP port 27918 and exploiting the flaw to overwrite an existing file outside of the intended directory and turn the arbitrary-file-write primitive into remote code execution. "The FortiSIEM gRPC QueryResultReq handler processes untrusted metadata without proper path validation," Horizon3.ai said. "By crafting metadata containing both path traversal sequences (../) and NUL-byte injection within gRPC's HTTP/2 and HPACK encoding layers, an attacker can write arbitrary files to the file system." The problem stems from a case of unsafe path construction within a function named SendQueryResult(), which passes a user-supplied "query-id" parameter directly without sufficient validation. In other words, an attacker can leverage this flaw to include directory traversal sequences such as "../" and escape that directory. However, this only allows an attacker to navigate to a directory of their choice and write to it, but not to opt for a file name because the program automatically adds its own file name "result-<source IP address>-0-0-<id>.dat," where <id> is a counter value controlled by the server. That's where a second weakness enters the picture: a null byte ("\0") can be embedded in the "query-id" parameter, causing the operating system to interpret it as a string terminator and discard everything that comes after it. This, in turn, results in the appended file name suffix being ignored when the path is passed to the file-opening function. An attacker could exploit this behavior to craft a "query-id" value with "\0" placed such that it's preceded by the actual file name to be overwritten – i.e., "../../../../../opt/charting/redishb.sh\0..." The file in question is a shell script that performs health checks on the Redis service and is run every 60 seconds by a cron job. "The write lands on the exact path that preceded the null byte," Zach Hanley, Chief Attack Engineer at Horizon3.ai, said. "Pointed at an existing file, this overwrites it in place, keeping the original owner and permissions; a second variant uses two requests to create a brand-new file with an exact name."

d57pzn.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 20, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security Palo Alto Networks has disclosed that it's continuing to observe exploitation of a now-patched security flaw impacting PAN-OS and Prisma Access by ransomware actors. The activity relates to CVE-2026-0257 (CVSS score: 7.8), an authentication bypass flaw that could be exploited by bad actors to set up unauthorized VPN connections. It was patched by Palo Alto Networks in May 2026 and was added by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CSIA) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on May 13, 2026. "Ransomware operators exploiting CVE-2026-0257 include Spikey Scorpius (aka Qilin) and Tarnished Scorpius (aka INC)," Unit 42 researchers said in an update shared on Monday. The development comes days after ReliaQuest said it detected both Qilin and Settra ransomware groups actively exploiting the flaw in financially-motivated attacks. According to Unit 42, the threat actors are weaponizing the flaw to gain an initial foothold into corporate networks, and then bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls to establish a VPN session. Upon setting up a VPN session, the attackers have been found to engage in the following post-compromise activity - Conduct internal network reconnaissance using dual-use remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools. Move laterally across the network via RDP and SMB. Stage additional tooling for credential harvesting, data exfiltration, and ransomware deployment. Attacks mounted by these groups are said to have targeted a wide range of sectors, including education, financial services, healthcare, high technology, hospitality, manufacturing, professional and legal services, government, transportation and logistics, utilities and energy, and retail. "The most significant evolution in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is the direct pivot to the virtualization layer," Unit 42 said. "In one notable case, attackers moved from the compromised VPN gateway to the vCenter management appliance. From there, they disabled security controls on ESXi hypervisors (execInstalledOnly) and used a custom tool to perform offline credential dumping directly against a domain controller's virtual disk (VMDK)." This approach, the network security vendor added, circumvents in-guest endpoint detection and response (EDR) and security protections, allowing the threat actors to obtain domain-wide credentials. Attackers have also been observed chaining the initial access method with other exploit tools, including efforts to target Veeam backup infrastructure by abusing known flaws (CVE-2023-27532) to inflict maximum damage. It's worth noting that Qilin's exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 was previously flagged by Arctic Wolf in July 2026, with attacks ranging from rapid encryption-only operations to full double-extortion. Besides applying the latest fixes, Palo Alto Networks is recommending that organizations proactively hunt for indicators of compromise and initiate appropriate incident response protocols if successful gateway-connected events are detected.

1r9tgcc.text: A Chinese-speaking criminal pointed autonomous AI agents at company websites and let them break in with almost no help, and a security researcher watched it happen because the operators left their control panels open on the internet. The agents tried more than 1,200 sites and reached websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including farm-equipment maker Deere, appliance company SharkNinja and engine maker Cummins, according to Reuters, which reviewed the attacker's own records to identify them. How much data, if any, was taken is not known. The researcher, Snorre Fagerland of the security firm NorForge, found the operations by scanning the internet for exposed copies of Cairn, an open-source AI tool popular with hackers. Beginning around October 2, he found about two dozen Cairn instances being used maliciously, which let him read the attackers' work in real time. He set out the findings on Monday, and Reuters, which saw the report before publication, named the victims from its own review of the attacker's activity. Cairn gives AI agents a starting point and a goal, then lets them work toward it step by step. The agents post what they find to a shared board, and the human operator can add hints along the way. It was built for authorized penetration testing and does other jobs too, but here it was pointed at online shops without permission. Cairn's author, who posts as "le1xia0," told Reuters the tool was not designed for hacking attacks and that harmful use was not their intention. What the agents did, and who was hit NorForge grouped the exposed panels into three clusters and judged more than 20 of them likely to be malicious. The busiest cluster, which NorForge calls AIA0001, is Chinese-language and links 14 panels to more than 1,100 attack projects. Its aim seems to be lasting access to shop and payment systems for later use, NorForge said, with targets in the United States, Japan and Australia. A typical task told the agents to find a way to run code on a shop and then plant a web shell uploader. That is a form that saves uploaded files, not one that runs commands, and attackers can swap it for something worse at any time. NorForge checked one claimed break-in, at a large hardware-parts vendor, and found the web shell live. It independently confirmed the compromise of one very large US retailer, in which the agents found the single cookie setting that selected a vulnerable backend server. The three named companies told Reuters the damage was limited. Deere said it took steps to fix the problem and had no sign that sensitive information was accessed. SharkNinja said the attack hit a standalone product-support site and that it had contained the threat. Cummins said it was investigating a report of a possible attack on a website run by one of its vendors. Two smaller businesses also told Reuters they were compromised. One documented intrusion, by the agent's own account, worked through unauthorized write access to a memcached session store, unsafe handling of saved PHP objects, and a weakness in old Zend Framework code. The paths differ from victim to victim, so this is one chain, not a single method. Cheap, fast, and largely unsupervised The instructions were short. The Chinese-speaking operator sketched out preferred tactics in fewer than 100 Chinese characters, Reuters reported, and the agents went from there. Successful break-ins took a little under 23 hours on average, NorForge found, and the overall success rate across the tools it saw was around 10%, though it cautioned the clusters chase different goals and are not directly comparable. The cost was low, but the figures are rough. NorForge put the average at about $5 a task, counting attempts that failed or ended early, and said the uncertainty is considerable. Fagerland separately told Reuters the whole campaign had used about $5,000 worth of tokens, or roughly $50 per successful hack. All the AIA0001 tasks ran under a worker named claudecode_deepseek-v4.1-flash, which could point to a DeepSeek V4.1 Flash model driven by Anthropic's Claude Code. Neither the researcher nor Reuters confirmed the models, and Reuters said only that the campaign appeared to use DeepSeek and Claude Code. The open panels leak the victims' secrets too Leaving a Cairn panel open is a separate problem from the break-ins. The panels show who is being attacked, what weaknesses were found, and which credentials and keys were taken, so having your site tested on an open instance can expose your secrets, whatever the test's outcome. NorForge ran the secrets scanner Trufflehog over the panel data and found hundreds of secrets, 11% of which it verified as still valid. The panels also appear to expose the full set of the tool's controls, including the ability to start and stop projects, feed in new data, and point agents to different targets. NorForge said it did not test whether those controls work without a login. A second, English-language cluster went further and exposed the operators' own SSH logins to their staging servers; NorForge said it did not log in. The exposure is not only a criminal problem. NorForge also found apparently legitimate penetration-testing firms that had left real client tests on unsecured panels, putting their customers' data at the same risk. What to check, and where this came from Defenders can act on a few points: Exposed panels. Agent control panels of this kind often answer on port 8000, so an exposed one without a login is worth hunting for. Stray upload forms. An unexpected file-upload form sitting in a hidden directory is the foothold these agents aimed for. Magento patching. A worker directory NorForge browsed held a proof-of-concept for a critical Magento flaw, StyleSmuggler (CVE-2026-75650), and a test lab for it. There is no evidence it was used in these break-ins, but any shop still on an affected build should apply Adobe's hotfix for it: Adobe Commerce 2.4.4 through 2.4.9, or Magento Open Source 2.4.6 through 2.4.9. NorForge's search followed a September report by Gambit Security, a separate campaign in which a criminal used Cairn alongside two other AI tools to steal credit cards; that report is what first flagged Cairn on an attacker's server. No source links the two operations. NorForge said it is working with Reuters to warn victims and is asking hosting firms to take the panels down, an effort it said depends on how the hosts respond.

1hrqxla.text: The iPhone of Vladan Đokić, rector of the University of Belgrade and a prominent supporter of Serbia's student protest movement, was infected with NSO Group's Pegasus spyware in 2026, the Citizen Lab said on October 19. The finding came six days before Serbia's October 25 snap parliamentary election. The infection used a zero-click exploit, meaning Đokić did not have to tap a link or open a file for it to work. The lab found the infection with high confidence, but its note provides no date within 2026, does not identify who was behind the attack, and notes that its investigation is ongoing. The election was called in September after nearly two years of protests that began when a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024, killing 16 people. The Citizen Lab, a research group at the University of Toronto, analyzed forensic artifacts from the phone at Đokić's request, working with the Serbian digital-rights group SHARE Foundation. SHARE led the investigation of an earlier wave of Serbian cases made public in September. A second case concerns Rade Bajić, a senior prosecutorial associate at Serbia's Public Prosecutor's Office for Organized Crime who worked on the "Generalštab" corruption investigation into a Kushner-linked property project in Belgrade. Bajić received an Apple Threat Notification on August 13 and a reminder on August 27. Apple sends these alerts when it detects activity consistent with an attack by mercenary spyware, the commercial hacking tools that companies such as NSO sell to governments, and it does not say who is behind the attacks. The Citizen Lab treats a notification as a high-confidence sign that Bajić's phone was likely targeted. Its forensic analysis of the device is ongoing, and the note does not say whether the phone was infected. The Generalštab case concerns the removal of heritage protection from Belgrade's bombed-out former army General Staff complex to clear the way for a luxury development backed by a company linked to Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law. In December 2025, prosecutors charged Culture Minister Nikola Selaković and three other officials with abuse of office and falsifying documents in the case, the Associated Press reported. Bajić says he was taken off the investigation in November 2025 without explanation, and in February he spoke about the case at a protest called by student activists outside Serbia's Constitutional Court. The lab's note does not say what, if anything, was taken from the rector's phone. Pegasus gives whoever operates it the same access as the phone's owner, including private and encrypted messages, and can switch on the microphone and camera without the owner knowing, according to the lab's analysis of the September case. Đokić called the spyware on his phone "another attempt of intimidation" in an English-language statement published by the university, and demanded an independent investigation without delay, with its results made public and whoever installed and used the spyware prosecuted. Police raided the rector's offices on March 31 and seized computers and servers, he said at the time. The Security Information Agency (BIA), Serbia's civilian security service, dismissed the September allegations that students and opposition politicians had been spied on as "purely trivial sensationalism" in a statement on September 3, as translated by the broadcaster N1, and said it operates strictly within Serbian law. The two cases extend a wave that SHARE reported on September 2, when it said at least 14 people in Serbia, including student activists, an opposition MP and a local councilor, had been targeted with spyware since the start of the year. Twelve of them had received Apple Threat Notifications in August, the month Apple warned users in 110 countries. One was Jelena Kontić, a student whose Pegasus infection the Citizen Lab confirmed. The other two had a new version of NoviSpy, an Android spyware, installed on their phones. By the Citizen Lab's count, the two new cases bring the number of people in Serbian civil society publicly known to have been targeted or infected with mercenary spyware this year to at least 16. Amnesty International reported in December 2024 that NoviSpy was configured to send stolen data to a server whose IP address belonged to the BIA and was installed on activists' and journalists' phones during police questioning, after the devices were unlocked with Cellebrite forensic tools. Lawyers for Kontić filed a criminal complaint on October 6 against unidentified individuals in the BIA and the police, as well as people responsible at NSO Group. Pegasus is sold only to governments and state agencies, SHARE says, and the complaints already filed over spyware in Serbia have brought no effective action. The note does not name the flaw used against Đokić's phone or say whether current iOS releases block it, so there is no case-specific fix to install. The lab's advice for people at risk because of who they are or what they do: Turn on Lockdown Mode on your iPhone and keep iOS up to date. If you receive an Apple Threat Notification, assume the phone is infected until an expert has checked it, and get help at once: SHARE Foundation in Serbia, or Access Now's Digital Security Helpline elsewhere. Have close contacts, such as family members and people they work with, screened for spyware too.

d2s85l.text: A public proof of concept has exposed a flaw in Telegram Desktop that could let attackers steal local files and take over accounts after a user clicks a crafted external link. Tracked as CVE-2026-107181, the vulnerability affects versions before 7.2.9 and carries a CVSS 4.0 severity rating of 8.6 (High). Researcher Beaksec published the technical write-up on October 3, 2026, and updated it on October 7. VulnCheck assigned the CVE that day. The reported attack reaches Telegram’s local session data, making account takeover possible when the victim has not enabled a local passcode. The weakness lies in how Telegram Desktop handles links opened outside the app. When Telegram is already running, another instance passes the link to it through a local communication channel, known as inter-process communication, or IPC. That channel failed to escape a character used to separate records. An attacker could place the character inside a crafted link and make Telegram read part of the link as another command. The CVE record classifies this as CWE-143, improper handling of record delimiters. PoC Released for Telegram Desktop Flaw According to ThreatWire’s research, the injected command could access an outdated internal helper designed for release publishing. The helper could read local files and send them to a chat without permission checks or user confirmation. The result is file theft through Telegram itself. Stolen session files could let an attacker reuse the victim’s logged-in account. Earlier reporting on Telegram account hijacking through voicemail shows another route to account loss, but that method is separate from this Desktop vulnerability. The researcher demonstrated the chain on Windows using Telegram Desktop 6.9.3 and reported that it remained present through 7.2.8. Although the CVE covers Telegram Desktop generally, the write-up does not demonstrate the attack on macOS or Linux. The link must be opened outside Telegram, such as from a browser. Links clicked inside Telegram follow a different processing path and are not affected. A browser may also ask for permission before launching the desktop app. The demonstrated chain depends on automatic group file downloads and settings that allow anyone to add the victim to a group. These conditions matter when judging the “one-click” claim. Previous EvilVideo coverage also highlighted download settings, although that issue affected Telegram for Android rather than Desktop. Telegram fixed the issue in commit db3405699f on September 16 and released version 7.2.9 on September 17. The reported changes remove the legacy helper, escape the record separator, and strengthen handling of mixed record types. The release notes mention only a rendering fix, not the security issue. No vendor security advisory is identified in the supplied reporting. The CVSS 3.1 score is 8.1, while CVSS 4.0 gives 8.6. Both ratings describe the same flaw. Users should update every Telegram Desktop installation to 7.2.9 or later. Until then, restrict group invitations, stop automatic downloads, and enable a local passcode. Treat unexpected browser prompts to open Telegram cautiously. As of October 9, the supplied reporting identifies no known exploitation or CISA KEV listing. A public PoC demonstrates feasibility, not confirmed attacks. The public write-up should not be mistaken for independent attack confirmation. Users who suspect exposure should end other active sessions and review chats for unexpected file uploads. Stops threats before impact with 21 min faster MTTR. We scored ten options with context and elimination weighted above raw detection. Evaluating scanners alongside the Top 10 Best Container Security Tools in 2026 reveals that static vulnerability counts alone do not prevent attackers who compromise container hosts through misconfigurations. Aqua’s Trivy takes 1 as the free floor everyone should run; Sysdig and Wiz complete a podium built on making findings mean something. How We Scored (Methodology) Research-based: detection quality, SBOM support, context/prioritization, registry/workflow fit, pricing transparency. No lab testing; no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Weights: context quality 30%, detection/SBOM 25%, workflow fit 20%, pricing accessibility 15%, elimination strategy 10%. Even as organizations maintain vigilance following threats like the Trivy supply chain attack on public registries, its multi-target engine remains the baseline floor no CI/CD pipeline should lack. Minimal, continuously rebuilt, and cryptographically signed images resolve what CVE counts miss about container security by collapsing false positives and shrinking software bills of materials before deployment. Standout features: Hardened bases; provenance included; FIPS variants. Pros: Queue elimination. Cons: Migration engineering; per-image cost. Bottom line: The base with nothing to report. 5.
